title: A forest floor holds the rain: how living things build a place together

summary.text: Pour a cup of pretend rain on bare soil, and the same amount on soil covered with dead leaves. Which one keeps the water, and which one sends brown mud down the slope? Your child tests three plates with a tea strainer, then tests how a blanket of leaves keeps soil damp. They find out how leaves, roots, worms and fungi together make a forest floor that holds water, which none of them could do alone. They read the signs of life on a trail, and meet the Bishnoi and the women of Reni, who stood up for trees. They also play a shared-pond game to learn how much we can take from nature and still let it grow back.
summary.art: Two plates tilted on a stack of books, one with bare brown soil and a brown stream running off it into a glass, one with soil under a loose layer of dead leaves and a thin clear trickle running into a glass.

intro.hook: Walk along a forest trail in the monsoon and the ground is soft, dark and wet under a thick carpet of dead leaves. Walk across a swept, cleared field in the same rain and the water runs off in brown streams. The rain is the same. Why does the ground behave so differently?
intro.text: Dead leaves look like rubbish, and a swept patch looks clean. But in a forest, leaves, roots, worms, termites and fungi all work on the ground at the same time. In this unit you build three small patches of ground on plates and pour pretend rain on them, to see for yourself what leaves do. Then you follow the same idea out along a trail. You read the signs that creatures leave behind, find out how people across India have protected groves and trees for hundreds of years, and ask how much we can take from nature and still let it grow back.
intro.art: A forest path in the monsoon with a thick layer of brown leaves on the ground and clear water trickling beside it, next to a bare cleared slope with muddy streams running down.

outcomes: I can explain that a place is a web of many kinds of links between living things, not only eating and being eaten.
I can name six kinds of links and give an example of each from a trail or a balcony.
I can run a fair test with a control, and use my measurements to explain how leaf litter and soil together hold rain.
I can explain how a layer of leaves keeps soil damp, and why farmers use mulch.
I can read the signs on a trail, such as a nibbled leaf, a mud tube or a dropping full of seeds, and say which link each sign shows.
I can describe some of the ways people in India have protected forests and trees, and say what science has found about them.
I can explain what sustainable means by using a rule about taking only what grows back, and say why shared things need rules.

terms.meaning: All the living beings of one place, together with the soil, water, air and sunlight they use. A pond is an ecosystem, and so is a forest or a balcony garden.
terms.example: A forest trail in the Western Ghats, with its trees, birds, insects, soil, streams and rain.
terms.art: A cross-section of a forest with trees, a stream, soil and animals, all labelled as one place.

terms.meaning: One kind of living being, such as a peepal tree, a house crow or a honeybee. Members of the same species can have young together.
terms.example: The house crow and the jungle crow are two species of crow.
terms.art: A house crow and a jungle crow side by side, with a label under each.

terms.meaning: The layer of fallen leaves, twigs, flowers and fruits that lies on the ground in a forest or a garden.
terms.example: The brown carpet of dry leaves under a neem tree.
terms.art: A hand lifting a handful of leaf litter, with a small beetle and a millipede on it.

terms.meaning: Rain water that does not soak into the ground but flows over the top of it, downhill.
terms.example: The brown stream that runs down a bare slope in the monsoon.
terms.art: Rain falling on a bare slope with arrows showing water flowing down over the surface.

terms.meaning: Water soaking down into the ground through the tiny gaps in the soil. A forest soil has many gaps, made by roots and by animals that dig.
terms.example: A puddle on loose, crumbly soil disappears within minutes.
terms.art: A cross-section of soil with arrows of water going down through root and worm tunnels.

terms.meaning: Soil being carried away by water or wind. Erosion makes hillsides thin and fills rivers and ponds with mud.
terms.example: Red mud washing into a village lane after a heavy rain on a bare slope.
terms.art: A bare slope with a gully cut into it and a muddy brown river at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A layer of leaves, straw or husk spread over soil to keep it damp, cool and covered.
terms.example: Coconut husk placed around a banana plant, or paddy straw spread over a vegetable bed.
terms.art: A banana plant with a thick ring of dry coconut husk around her base.

terms.meaning: A living being who changes a place so much that it becomes a home for others, or stops being one.
terms.example: Termites build tunnels and mounds. Snakes and other animals later live in the old mounds.
terms.art: A termite mound with a snake resting at one hole and a lizard at another.

terms.meaning: A plant letting water out as vapour through tiny holes in her leaves. This water goes into the air.
terms.example: A big tree can send hundreds of litres of water into the air on a hot day.
terms.art: A tree with small arrows of water vapour rising from every leaf into a cloud.

terms.meaning: A patch of forest that a community protects because it is holy to them. In Kerala it is called a kavu.
terms.example: The Mawphlang forest near Shillong in Meghalaya, which the Khasi people have protected for centuries.
terms.art: A patch of dark old forest standing in the middle of cleared farmland, with a small shrine at its edge.

terms.meaning: Used in a way that leaves enough for the future. Taking fish, wood or water no faster than they come back is sustainable.
terms.example: Cutting only the oldest bamboo stems, so the clump keeps growing.
terms.art: A bamboo clump with a few old stems cut and many new green shoots coming up.

terms.meaning: Something that a whole community shares and nobody owns alone, such as a village pond, a grazing field or a forest.
terms.example: A village pond that every family uses for water and fish.
terms.art: A village pond with families from different houses drawing water and a buffalo drinking at the edge.

explanations.concept: Six kinds of links in a web of life
explanations.definition: A web of life is all the living beings of one place and every link between them.
explanations.description: Eating is the link we notice first. But on a trail there are at least six kinds. One is food, such as a bulbul eating a berry. Two is shelter, such as a hornbill nesting in a tree hole. Three is help in making new plants, such as a bee carrying pollen. Four is travel, such as a bird carrying seeds in her gut. Five is clean-up, such as termites and fungi turning dead wood back into soil. Six is changing the place itself, such as roots holding a slope. One being can have all six links at once. Some links also hurt. A caterpillar eats a leaf, and two trees fight for the same light. A web has the harmful links too.
examples: A peepal tree feeds birds with her figs, shelters squirrels in her branches, and is held up by roots that also hold the soil.
A termite eats dead wood, shelters inside a mound, and digs tunnels that let rain water into the ground.
explanations.art: A tree with six coloured arrows leaving it, each going to a different animal, and each labelled with one kind of link.

explanations.concept: Ecosystem engineers: beings who change the place for everyone else
explanations.definition: An ecosystem engineer is a living being who changes a place so much that it becomes a home for others, or stops being one.
explanations.description: Some beings do more than eat and be eaten. They build the place. Termites dig tunnels and build mounds. Rain soaks into the tunnels, and snakes, mongooses and lizards later use the old mounds as homes. Earthworms eat soil and leaf bits and push the soil up. Charles Darwin studied worms for many years, from 1837. In 1881 he published a book showing that the worms in one field bring up many tonnes of soil a year. Tree roots grip the soil, so the soil does not slide. In dry riverbeds, elephants dig for water with their feet and trunks, and other animals drink from the holes they leave.
examples: Termites dig tunnels that let rain water sink into the ground.
Earthworms turn the soil over and open it up so that air and water can go in.
Elephants dig waterholes that smaller animals use.
explanations.art: A cut-away of soil showing a termite mound, worm tunnels and tree roots, with a snake in one mound and rain water running down the tunnels.

explanations.concept: The forest floor is a sponge made by many beings
explanations.definition: Leaf litter is the layer of fallen leaves, twigs and fruits on the ground. Together with soil, roots, animals and fungi, it soaks up rain and lets it go slowly.
explanations.description: Rain falls first on the leaves of the trees, which slow it down. Then it meets the leaf litter, which soaks up some water and breaks the fall of the drops. Under the litter, roots, worms and termites have made tunnels, so the water sinks in instead of running off. Thin threads of fungi and fine roots bind the soil crumbs together, so the soil does not wash away. The soil then holds water in its tiny gaps, like a sponge, and, in many places, lets it out slowly into springs and streams. On bare soil, raindrops break the crumbs. The mud fills the gaps and forms a crust, and the water runs off downhill, carrying the soil with it. This is erosion. Field measurements in many countries find that bare soil loses far more soil and water than covered soil.
examples: In many hill areas, streams below well-covered slopes keep flowing for longer after the rain. How strong this effect is differs from place to place.
Dams below cleared, bare hillsides often fill with mud faster than dams below forests.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a forest floor with rain falling on leaves, litter on the ground, root and worm tunnels, and water sinking slowly to a spring.

explanations.concept: A blanket on the soil: why a layer of leaves keeps soil damp
explanations.definition: Mulch is a layer of leaves, straw or husk spread over soil.
explanations.description: Sun and wind turn the water in soil into vapour. This is called evaporation. A layer of leaves shades the soil, keeps the wind off it and keeps it cooler, so less water escapes. The soil below stays damp for longer. Earthworms and many tiny animals come up into the damp soil, and they slowly pull the old leaves down and turn them into soil. Farmers in India use this idea. They spread paddy straw over vegetable beds, dry sugarcane leaves around young plants, and coconut husk around banana plants.
examples: Paddy straw spread on a vegetable bed in Tamil Nadu.
Coconut husk placed around a banana plant in Kerala.
explanations.art: Two garden beds side by side in the hot sun, one bare and cracked, the other covered with straw and dark with damp soil.

explanations.concept: Reading a trail: every sign is a link
explanations.definition: A sign is something a living being leaves behind, such as a track, a dropping, a feather, a nibbled leaf, a nest or a web.
explanations.description: On a nature trail you rarely see the animals. They hear you first. But they leave signs. A dropping full of seeds shows that an animal carried a plant's seeds. A notch in a leaf shows that something ate there. A thin mud tube up a tree shows that termites are cleaning up dead wood. A hole in a trunk shows a nest. Each sign shows one of the six links. To read a sign, ask three questions. Who might have made this? What were they doing? Who else gains from it? A beak and claws can also tell you about a bird: a thick short beak cracks seeds, and a long thin beak probes flowers or mud. Good trail rules protect both visitors and wildlife. Stay with your group. Walk quietly. Do not touch or pick plants and animals you do not know. Take your rubbish home.
examples: A purple dropping under a fig tree is full of fig seeds.
A tiny heap of sawdust under a tree shows a beetle tunnelling in the wood.
explanations.art: A child with a notebook and hand lens crouching beside a mud tube on a tree trunk, with a nibbled leaf and a feather nearby.

explanations.concept: Plants send water to the sky
explanations.description: A plant takes water from the soil with her roots and lets most of it go as vapour through tiny holes in her leaves. This is transpiration, and scientists have measured it well. The vapour rises, joins the air and may fall again as rain somewhere downwind. Studies of the Amazon forest estimate that roughly a quarter to a third of the rain there was once water that plants gave off, though estimates differ. What is debated is how far forests also pull in wet air from the sea. In 2007 two Russian scientists, Anastassia Makarieva and Victor Gorshkov, proposed a 'biotic pump'. They said that a big forest with strong transpiration lowers the air pressure over it and draws in moist sea air. Many atmospheric scientists doubt that this effect is strong, and the question is still being tested.
examples: A mature tree sends many litres of water into the air every day.
Clouds often gather over forested hills.

perspectives.explanation: Plants return a large share of the rain to the air, so cutting forests can reduce rain downwind. How large the effect is depends on the place.
Forests do more than recycle water. Their transpiration also pulls moist sea air inland, like a pump.
Winds and temperature differences matter more than the forest's pull. The pump idea needs more evidence.

explanations.art: A forest with arrows of water vapour rising from the leaves into clouds, and rain falling on hills far downwind.

explanations.concept: Is a forest one thing, or many things?
explanations.description: A forest holds water like a sponge, but no single member holds it. So is a forest like one body with many parts, or only many separate lives that happen to share a place? Scientists have argued about this for over a hundred years. The answer may be 'a little of both'.
examples: The forest sponge exists only when leaves, soil, roots and fungi are all there together.
A single tree can live on her own in a field, but a forest soil cannot form without many beings.

perspectives.explanation: A plant community is like one living body. It is born, grows up and ripens, and its parts work as a team.
Each plant lives by her own needs and her own luck. A community is a chance meeting of many lives, not a body.
On the scale of the whole Earth, living and non-living parts together keep the air and the oceans fairly steady, a bit like a body. This 'Gaia' idea is still debated.

explanations.art: A forest drawn twice, once as a single large tree-shaped body with organs, once as many separate trees and animals each with their own outline.

explanations.concept: Sacred groves: forests kept by a community
explanations.definition: A sacred grove is a patch of forest that a community protects because it is holy to them.
explanations.description: Across India there are thousands of sacred groves. In Kerala they are called kavu, in Karnataka devarakadu, and in Maharashtra devrai. The Mawphlang sacred forest near Shillong in Meghalaya has been looked after by the Khasi people for centuries. In many groves, people may not cut a tree, hunt, or even carry away dead leaves. Many groves hold old trees and plants that have become rare outside. Some feed springs and streams. In 1975 the Indian ecologist Madhav Gadgil and V. D. Vartak wrote a paper asking for these groves to be kept. Scientists still ask how much groves protect nature, and how long they will last.
examples: A kavu in Kannur, Kerala, with old trees standing in the middle of farmland.
The Mawphlang forest near Shillong in Meghalaya.

perspectives.who: The families who keep the grove
perspectives.explanation: The forest belongs to the gods or the ancestors. Taking anything from it is wrong, and this rule has protected it for generations.
Groves work as small nature reserves. They often hold plants and animals that are rare outside, and they often protect water.
Many groves are small and shrinking, and belief in the old rules is fading in some places. A grove alone cannot save a whole landscape.

explanations.art: An old dark patch of forest with a small stone shrine, standing in the middle of bright green farmland, with a spring running from its foot.

explanations.concept: People who stood up for trees: the Bishnoi and the women of Reni
explanations.definition: A movement to protect trees is an organised effort by ordinary people who refuse to let trees be cut.
explanations.description: The Bishnoi people of Rajasthan follow rules, set down in the 1400s, not to cut green trees or hurt wild animals. Tradition says that in 1730, at the village of Khejarli near Jodhpur, the king's men came to cut khejri trees for fuel. A woman named Amrita Devi hugged a tree to stop them, and many villagers did the same. Tradition says about 363 people died. The king then stopped the cutting. In 1974 in the village of Reni, in the Garhwal Himalaya, the men were away when contractors came to fell trees. Women led by Gaura Devi stood in front of the trees and would not move, and the contractors left. Reni became the best-known event of the Chipko movement. Chipko comes from the Hindi word for 'stick' or 'hug'. In 1980 the government banned the felling of green trees for 15 years in the Himalayan hills of Uttar Pradesh, where Reni was then. Today Reni is in Uttarakhand.
examples: The khejri tree, which gives shade and food in the Thar desert, is still protected by Bishnoi villages.
Women in the Himalaya continued to protect forests long after Reni.
explanations.art: A woman with her arms around a khejri tree in the desert and villagers beside her, facing men with axes.

explanations.concept: Sustainable: taking only what grows back
explanations.definition: Sustainable means used in a way that leaves enough for the future.
explanations.description: Everything alive can be used up if we take it faster than it comes back. A bamboo clump grows new stems every year. If you cut only the oldest stems, the clump keeps going. If you cut them all, she dies. A fish pond works in the same way. If you leave enough fish to breed, the pond refills. If you take the breeding fish, the pond empties. This is why Kerala stops trawling at sea for weeks in the monsoon, when fish are breeding. Water works in the same way. Johads, the earth dams of Rajasthan, and the temple tanks of Tamil Nadu slow the rain and let it sink into the ground, so wells refill. An old Indian hymn to the Earth, in the Atharvaveda, asks that whatever is dug from her may quickly grow back.
examples: Cutting only the oldest bamboo stems.
A fishing ban in the breeding season.
Johads and tanks that refill wells.
explanations.art: A bamboo clump with a farmer cutting only the tallest, oldest stems, while young shoots rise around her.

explanations.concept: Shared things: who keeps them safe?
explanations.description: A village pond, a grazing field and a forest are commons. In 1968 the biologist Garrett Hardin argued that people with a shared field will always add one more cow until the grass is gone. He called this 'the tragedy of the commons'. Elinor Ostrom, a political scientist, looked at real villages. Many had shared a meadow, a forest or an irrigation canal for hundreds of years without ruining it. They had rules about who could take how much. People watched each other, and cheats were warned and then fined. In 2009 she won the Nobel Prize in Economics for this work, the first woman to do so. Both are right in part. Without rules, a shared thing is often used up. With good rules made by the people who use it, it can last.
examples: The village pond or the gochar, the grazing land that every family may use.
An irrigation canal where families take turns.

perspectives.explanation: If everyone takes a little more for themselves, the shared thing is destroyed. It needs a private owner or a government to protect it.
Villagers who use a shared thing can make and keep their own rules. Many have done so for centuries.

explanations.art: A village pond with a notice of rules painted on a wall beside it, and families taking turns to draw water.

agreed.text: A forest floor of leaf litter, roots and soil animals soaks up rain and lets it go slowly.
agreed.evidence: Measurements on covered and bare plots in many countries find that bare soil loses much more water and soil in heavy rain.

agreed.text: A layer of mulch keeps soil damp for longer than bare soil.
agreed.evidence: Farmers and scientists have compared mulched and bare beds. Mulched soil loses less water to evaporation.

agreed.text: Most places hold many kinds of links between living beings, not only food links.
agreed.evidence: Studies of pollination, seed travel, nesting and soil show links of many kinds between the same species.

agreed.text: Plants give off large amounts of water as vapour, and this water becomes part of the rain downwind.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of rain, humidity and plant water use in the Amazon and other forests show a large recycled share.

agreed.text: Earthworms and termites change the soil and the land.
agreed.evidence: In 1881 Charles Darwin weighed the soil that worms bring up. Later measurements of termite tunnels show that rain sinks in faster there.

agreed.text: Shared resources can last for centuries when the people who use them make and keep rules.
agreed.evidence: Elinor Ostrom and others collected hundreds of cases from many countries, including meadows, forests and canals.

challenging.claim: Dead leaves on the ground are rubbish, and a clean-swept ground is healthier.
challenging.who: Many gardeners and some city rules.
challenging.for: A swept yard looks tidy and has fewer places for some pests to hide.
challenging.against: Leaf litter soaks up rain, keeps soil damp and feeds worms and fungi. Bare soil washes away and dries out.

challenging.claim: A forest is one living body.
challenging.who: Frederic Clements, early in the 1900s, and some later ecologists.
challenging.for: Many parts depend on each other, and the whole does things, such as holding water, that no part does alone.
challenging.against: Plants and animals live by their own needs and do not share a body or a goal. Communities change when the climate changes, and their members move separately.

challenging.claim: Forests make rain by pulling in wet air from the sea (the biotic pump).
challenging.for: Forests give off a lot of vapour, and rain does fall more over forests in some places.
challenging.against: Many atmospheric scientists find that winds and temperature differences do most of the work.

challenging.claim: Shared things are always ruined, unless someone owns them or a government rules them.
challenging.for: Overfished seas and overgrazed fields exist where nobody set rules.
challenging.against: Elinor Ostrom found many shared meadows, forests and canals that lasted for hundreds of years under village rules.

challenging.claim: Sacred groves protect all the nature around them.
challenging.who: Some writers on nature and culture.
challenging.for: Many groves hold old trees and rare plants, and some feed springs.
challenging.against: Many groves are small and shrinking, and the land around them is often cleared.

big_questions.q: The forest floor holds water, yet no single leaf, root or worm holds it. So what is holding the water?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Forest Floor Test. What did the plate with only soil do, and what did the plate with only leaves do?

big_questions.q: Is a forest one thing with many parts, or many things that happen to share a place?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the forest does that no one part does. Then think about what each part wants for herself.

big_questions.q: A crow, a termite and a frog all live in the same field. Do they live in the same world?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one senses: smell, sound, heat, light. Are they seeing the same field differently, or seeing different fields?

big_questions.q: People protected groves because they were holy. Does it matter why a forest is protected, if the forest is saved?
big_questions.hint: Think about the families who keep the grove, and the scientists who study it. What does each say?

big_questions.q: If the village pond belongs to everyone, who should decide how much each person takes?
big_questions.hint: Think about the Shared Pond game. What happened when you talked first, and when you did not?

big_questions.q: Is a city, or your building, also part of the web of life?
big_questions.hint: Think of the crow's nest made of wire, the pigeons on the ledge and the ants in the kitchen.

big_questions.q: Who counts as 'someone' in a web: only the ones we can see, or also the soil, the fungi and the rain?
big_questions.hint: Think about the plates in the Forest Floor Test. Who did the work there? In a forest, who does work that nobody sees?

story.title: The Well That Never Dried
story.note: A made-up story. Devika, Ammamma and Sreeja Chechi are not real people. Sacred groves called kavu are real, and there are many in north Kerala. Leaf litter and soil really do soak up and hold rain, and bare, swept ground really does shed it as muddy water. Whether one grove feeds one well depends on the land, so that part is imagined.
text: Devika came to her grandmother's house in Kannur in April, when the whole of Kerala was waiting for rain. The paddy fields were cracked. The red road was the colour of old brick. Even the crows sat in the shade with their beaks open.

Behind Ammamma's house the land climbed to a small, dark hill of old trees. This was the kavu. Nobody cut a branch there. Nobody picked a flower, or took a twig, or even carried away a dead leaf. "Gods live in there," said Ammamma. "We do not take from their house."

On the second morning Devika took a steel bucket to the well. She expected to see the bottom. Instead the water was only an arm's length down, cool and clear. Next door, Sreeja Chechi's well had been dry for three weeks. She was carrying water from the school tap in two plastic pots.

"Why does ours have water?" Devika asked. "Because of the kavu," said Ammamma, as if it were obvious. "That is not an answer," said Devika. She had noticed that grown-ups sometimes say because when they mean I do not know. Ammamma only laughed. "Then find a better one."

So Devika walked round both pieces of land. Sreeja Chechi's compound was spotless. Every leaf had been swept and burned, and every little bush cut down. It looked like a courtyard. Then Devika climbed into the kavu. Here everything was a mess. Leaves lay ankle-deep, brown on top and black underneath. Mud tubes ran up the tree trunks. A line of ants vanished under a rotting log. The air smelled of wet earth, though it had not rained for two months.

Devika knelt and pushed her hand under the leaves. The ground was cool and damp, and laced with fine white threads. A worm slid away from her fingers. She scooped up a handful of the black leaf-mould and squeezed it. Water ran out between her fingers, as from a wet cloth. She looked at her hand. In it were leaves from a dozen kinds of tree, roots finer than hair, white threads of fungus, a worm, and a beetle the size of a grain of rice. None of these was a well.

That evening the first storm of the summer arrived. The sky went black, the air smelled of dust, and then the rain came so hard that it bounced. Devika stood on the verandah with Ammamma. Down the lane ran a river the colour of tea with too much milk. It was red, thick and fast, and it came from Sreeja Chechi's neat compound. It was carrying her good soil away.
Then Devika looked the other way. Where the kavu met the lane, a thin trickle ran out from under the leaves. It was slow, and almost clear. Most of the rain had simply gone into the hill.
"The hill isn't drinking the rain," Devika said slowly. "The hill is holding it, and letting it out a little at a time. That is how the well still has water in April."

Ammamma said nothing, but her eyes crinkled. "My mother told me never to take even a dead leaf from the kavu," she said. "She said the gods would be angry. I never asked her what the gods were made of." Devika thought about it. "Leaves," she said. "Roots. Worms. Fungus." Ammamma laughed. "That is a great many gods. No wonder they are strong."

The next morning Devika helped Sreeja Chechi carry her pots. She did not say I told you so. She said, "Chechi, what if you did not burn your leaves? What if you put them round the coconut palms, like a blanket?" Sreeja Chechi looked at the leaves, and at her bare red ground, and at her empty well. "A blanket," she said. "My mother did that." She sighed. "We were so proud of being clean."

By the end of the week, each coconut palm in the compound stood in a patch of untidy brown leaves. It was not a kavu. It would take years to become one. But when the next rain came, Devika saw the water move slowly across that compound, instead of running off.
story.epiphany: The hill never drank the rain. Leaves, roots, worms and fungi together held the rain, and let it out slowly.
ask: What job does each part of a forest floor do for the water, and what is lost if one part is missing?
The rule in the kavu is that nothing is ever taken from it. How does that rule help the kavu, whatever the reason for the rule?
How could you find out whether leaves under a tree keep the ground damp, without harming the tree?
