roots.context: In the Forest Floor Test you poured pretend rain on soil and leaves. You also read signs on a trail and met people who protect trees. Now we ask what a forest floor shows about who does the work in a place, and what that tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Forest Floor Test, the plate with only soil lost the water fast, and so did the plate with only leaves. The plate with soil under leaves held it. No single part holds the water. The holding happens only when the parts are joined.
deep_truth.habit: We give the credit to one hero, such as the biggest tree, the tiger or the worm. We picture a place as a heap of separate things, each with its own job. But what a forest does for water belongs to the group, not to any member.
deep_truth.evidence: Compare the three plates in the Forest Floor Test. The usual result is that the plate with only soil and the plate with only leaves let more rain run off, and the plate with soil under leaves sends out clearer water. Write down what you really see. If your results differ, test again.

three.who_am_i: You are not one single thing. Your body holds trillions of cells and microbes, and none of them alone is you.
three.what_is_life: Life is not only single beings eating and growing. It is also the places that living beings make together, such as soil, a pond or a grove.
three.what_is_this_world: Rain, leaves, roots, worms and wells pass water to each other all the time. The water that fell on a leaf last week may be in a root, a worm or a spring today.

roots.thread: A forest looks like many separate trees, animals and fungi. The Forest Floor Test shows that some of what a forest does comes from the parts being joined, and not from any one part. The rain that lands on one leaf ends up, days later, in a root, a worm, a spring and a well. Indian and Buddhist teachers pictured the world as things linked to each other, as in Indra's net. A forest floor is a small place where you can watch these links at work: one rain is held by many beings together.

teachings.source: Indra's net, an image from the Avatamsaka Sutra tradition
teachings.teaching: Indra's net is pictured as a great net with a bright jewel at every knot. Each jewel shows the reflections of all the other jewels, and each of those shows all the rest. Nothing shines alone.
teachings.link: The forest floor is like this. Leaves, roots, worms and fungi each depend on the others. Take one away and the way the whole floor holds water changes.

teachings.teaching: The Isha Upanishad begins by saying that all of this world is filled by one source. So enjoy what is given, and do not grab what belongs to someone else.
teachings.link: In the Shared Pond game, grabbing more than the pond can give empties it for everyone. Taking only what is needed leaves enough for all.

teachings.source: Atharvaveda, the hymn to the Earth (Prithvi Sukta)
teachings.teaching: An old hymn to the Earth, in the Atharvaveda, asks that whatever is dug from her may quickly grow back, and that we may never hurt her heart.
teachings.link: This is the rule of sustainable living in one verse: take only what grows back.

science.text: Soil is held together by living beings. The tunnels, threads and crumbs that hold water are made by roots, worms, termites and fungi. Without them, soil is closer to dust.

Scientists still argue about whether a forest is best thought of as one whole that keeps itself steady, or as many separate lives. The Gaia idea of James Lovelock and Lynn Margulis says the whole Earth keeps itself steady.

other_view.who: Henry Gleason, an American plant ecologist (1926), and many ecologists since
other_view.view: A forest is not one thing. Each plant and animal lives by her own needs. A web is a name we give to many separate lives that happen to overlap, and the sponge is only the sum of what each part does.

practice.title: Follow one drop
practice.say: Sit near a plant, a tree or an open window. Breathe in slowly three times. Now picture one drop of rain landing on a leaf. See it slide to the soil. See it sink past the roots. See a root drink it. Where could it go next? Open your eyes and look at the plant. Her leaves are letting a little of that water go into the air right now.
practice.kid: Sit near a plant. Breathe in slowly three times. Picture one rain drop on a leaf. Follow it into the soil and into a root. Where does it go next?

ask: When leaves, roots and worms hold the water together, who is doing the holding?
If a forest can do what no part of it can do, are you also more than your parts?
Who should look after a place that nobody owns, and who should decide?
roots.art: Rain falling on a leaf, then following a thin line down into soil, past roots and a worm, into a spring and a well, drawn as one continuous line.

games.title: Sign Detective: who left this sign, and what link does it show?
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card describes a sign that a living being left on a trail. You work out who made it and which kind of link it shows.

printables.title: 24 sign cards: a sign on the front, and the answer on the back

items.f: A neat half-moon piece cut out of the edge of a rose leaf.
items.b: Who: a leafcutter bee. She cuts pieces of leaf to line the cells of her nest. Link: Shelter, because her nest is built from a plant. Look next: a small bee flying with a green piece held under her body.

items.f: Thin, winding white lines drawn on a citrus leaf, like scribbles.
items.b: Who: the tiny young of a moth or a fly, called a leaf miner, tunnelling between the top and bottom skin of the leaf. Link: Food. Look next: the line gets wider as the young one grows, so find the wide end.

items.f: A little heap of pale sawdust at the foot of a tree, with tiny holes in the bark above.
items.b: Who: the young of a wood-boring beetle, tunnelling inside the wood and pushing the dust out. Link: Food. Look next: old holes like this can later become homes for other small animals.

items.f: A thin brown tube of mud climbing a tree trunk or a wall.
items.b: Who: termites. The tube keeps them in the dark and damp while they travel. Link: Clean-up, because they eat dead wood and plants, and Changing the place, because their tunnels let water in. Look next: where the tube ends. Do not break it.

items.f: Little coils and heaps of fine, crumbly soil on the ground after rain.
items.b: Who: earthworms. The soil has passed through their bodies. Link: Changing the place, because their tunnels let air and water into the soil. Look next: a small hole nearby where a worm goes in.

items.f: A purple-black dropping full of tiny seeds under a fig or peepal tree.
items.b: Who: a bird or a fruit bat that ate figs. Link: Travel, because the seeds are carried away from the tree in the dropping. Look next: a young peepal growing on a wall or a roof.

items.f: A coconut hanging from the palm with a ragged, gnawed hole in its side.
items.b: Who: a rat or a squirrel. Link: Food. Look next: tiny tooth marks around the hole.

items.f: A round web with a spider waiting in the middle and a few small flies stuck in it.
items.b: Who: a spider that spins an orb web. Link: Food, because the web is a trap. Look next: some spiders rebuild the web every day.

items.f: A line of small black ants, all following the same path along a wall.
items.b: Who: ants following a smell trail laid by the ants before them. Link: Food, because they carry food back to the nest. Look next: where the line starts and where it ends.

items.f: A grey ball of fur and tiny bones under an old tree or in a barn.
items.b: Who: an owl. Owls swallow small animals whole and cough up the fur and bones they cannot digest. Link: Food. Look next: the bones show which small animals live nearby.

items.f: A hanging nest shaped like an upside-down flask, woven from grass on a palm or a babool tree.
items.b: Who: a male baya weaver bird. Link: Shelter, because the nest is woven from plants. Look next: many nests hang over water or on thorny trees where predators find it hard to reach.

items.f: A round hole in a tree trunk, with a bird flying in and out carrying insects.
items.b: Who: a bird with chicks, such as a woodpecker or a barbet. Link: Shelter. Look next: when the nest is empty, squirrels, bats or bees often move in.

items.f: Small hooked seeds and burrs stuck to your socks and clothes after the walk.
items.b: Who: plants such as grasses and herbs with hooked seeds. Link: Travel, because the seeds hitch a ride on fur, feathers and clothes. Look next: pick the seeds off and plant a few in a pot.

items.f: Heart-shaped prints split into two halves in wet mud at the edge of a stream.
items.b: Who: an animal with split hooves, such as a deer, a goat or a cow. Link: Food, because they come to eat and drink. Look next: dung nearby, which may hold seeds.

items.f: A fresh cow-dung pat with small round holes and beetles walking in and out.
items.b: Who: dung beetles. They roll or bury balls of dung to feed their young. Link: Clean-up, because they turn dung into food for their young and soil for plants. Look next: look for tiny balls buried under the pat. Look with your eyes and do not touch the dung.

items.f: A snail shell smashed open on a flat stone, with broken pieces all around.
items.b: Who: probably a bird, such as a thrush, that cracks snails on a stone. Link: Food. Look next: the same stone, which the bird may use again and again.

items.f: A leaf rolled up and stuck with silk threads, with a small caterpillar inside.
items.b: Who: a leaf-roller caterpillar. Link: Shelter and Food, because she lives in the rolled leaf and eats it. Look next: peek gently without touching, and leave the leaf as you found it, with her inside.

items.f: A small, hard, round lump about the size of a pea on a mango leaf.
items.b: Who: a tiny insect whose young make the leaf grow a swelling. Link: Shelter and Food, because the swelling is both a home and a meal for the young. Look next: use a lens and touch nothing.

items.f: A heap of fruit with half-moon bites and chewed lumps spat out, under a tall fruit tree in the morning.
items.b: Who: fruit bats or monkeys. Link: Food and Travel, because they eat the fruit and may carry seeds away. Look next: look up for bats hanging in the tree by day. Do not touch fallen fruit or bats.

items.f: Dark, damp soil under a pile of dead leaves, with pale, dry soil all around.
items.b: Who: the dead leaves themselves. They shade the soil and keep the wind off. Link: Changing the place. Look next: ask a grown-up to lift the leaves with a stick, look for small animals, then put the leaves back. Do not use your bare hands.

items.f: A loud buzzing around a tree in flower, and yellow petals scattered on the ground.
items.b: Who: bees and other insects drinking nectar. Link: Making new plants, because they carry pollen from flower to flower. Look next: yellow dust on a bee's legs.

items.f: Tiny bird prints on wet sand at the edge of a pond, with three toes pointing forwards and a small one pointing backwards.
items.b: Who: a bird that walks at the water's edge, such as a sandpiper. Link: Food, because the bird hunts for small animals in the mud. Look next: where the prints stop, because the bird may have flown off.

items.f: A crow's nest high in a city tree, built of twigs, wire and strips of plastic.
items.b: Who: a crow. Link: Shelter, with building material that people left behind. Look next: how many different kinds of things are in the nest.

items.f: A fallen log covered with shelf-shaped fungi and tiny holes, with beetles walking over it.
items.b: Who: fungi and beetles. Link: Clean-up, because they break the dead wood down into soil. Look next: ask a grown-up to lift a piece of bark with a stick, look for small animals underneath, then put it back. Do not use your bare hands.

printables.title: 6 link tokens: Food, Shelter, Making new plants, Travel, Clean-up, Changing the place

rules: Cut out the 24 sign cards and the 6 link tokens. Lay the tokens face up. Shuffle the cards and stack them face down.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads only the front aloud.
Every other player says who probably made the sign, and picks one link token. Playing alone, you do both.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. A player scores 1 point for a sensible guess about who made the sign, such as an insect or a bird, and 1 point for a link that the back mentions.
Take turns to be the reader. Play 10 cards. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to score 12 points out of 20.

setup.art: Twenty-four sign cards stacked face down and six link tokens laid face up in a row on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Lay the tokens out. Stack the cards face down.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while a parent holds up a link token.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front of one card. Everyone picks a link token.

setup.art: A card turned over to show the answer, with points being counted on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over. Score the points.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards and stack them face down. Lay the six link tokens in a row. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: We are trail detectives. Each card shows a sign that a living being left behind. Your job is to say who made it and which link it shows.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Put out the six link tokens.
flow.parent: The six links are Food, Shelter, Making new plants, Travel, Clean-up and Changing the place. Read them out loud before you start. With 2 to 4 players, the reader changes every card, so each child reads in turn. Children may cut the cards with blunt-tipped scissors, or the parent cuts them. One child can lay out the tokens while another shuffles.
flow.context: This is the set-up step of Sign Detective. You prepare the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Read the front of one card aloud, and nothing else. Everyone says who made the sign and picks a token. Read the back and give points. Play ten cards.
flow.say: Read me the sign. I will say who I think made it, and I will pick a link. Then we check the back. There is one point for a sensible guess about who made it, and one point for a link that the back mentions.
flow.kid: Read a card. Say who made the sign. Pick a link token. Check the back.

ask.q: Which clue on the front helped you most?
good: The shape of the hole or the tube.
The place where it was found.
What was inside the dropping.

check.q: A thin mud tube climbs a tree trunk. Which link does it show most clearly?
check.why: Termites build the tube to travel safely while they eat dead wood. That is clean-up. A mud tube has nothing to do with pollen or with seeds.

flow.context: This is the main step of Sign Detective. You guess who left each sign and which link it shows.

flow.do: Add up the points. Choose the sign that was hardest to read. Talk about who else gains from that sign.
flow.say: Which sign was hardest to read? Who else gains from it? On a real trail, we look first and touch nothing.
flow.kid: Count your points. Which sign was hardest? Who else gains from it?
flow.parent: Good answers see a second link. A dropping full of seeds shows food for the animal and travel for the plant.
flow.context: This is the last step of Sign Detective. You count points and think about the signs.

experiments.title: Forest Floor Test: which plate keeps the rain?
experiments.question: Pretend rain falls on three sloping plates: bare soil, soil with dry leaves on top, and dry leaves with no soil. How much water runs off each plate, and how muddy is it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which plate will send off the most water, and which will send off the muddiest water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every plate is the same size, is lifted to the same slope, and gets the same amount of rain from the same strainer. Plate A, bare soil, is the starting point. Plate B changes one thing from A: dry leaves on top. Plate C has the same leaves as B but no soil. Because each plate differs in only one way, a difference in the runoff comes from that one thing.

materials.item: 3 identical large flat plates with a very low rim or none, such as flat steel plates or tray lids
about 2 tumblers (400 millilitres) of dry garden soil, crumbled, with stones removed (ordinary garden or pot soil works better than fine sand)
2 handfuls of dry leaves, crushed into bits about the size of a postage stamp (dried used tea leaves will do)
a tea strainer
a measuring jug or a tumbler marked at 200 millilitres
6 clear glasses or jars, labelled A, B and C twice
a stack of books about 5 centimetres high
a strip of folded kitchen foil or thin plastic (cut from an old plastic bottle or file cover) for each plate, to make a chute into the glass; paper goes soggy
a sheet of white paper, a clock or phone timer, a bucket or tray for spills, and the results table

experiments.safety: Do the test over a bucket, a sink or a bathroom floor, because it is messy. Wash your hands after touching soil. Do not put soil or leaves near your mouth. Keep the dry leaves away from any flame.
experiments.record: Write the seconds until the first drop, the millilitres that ran off in each rain, and how muddy the water was. Then draw a bar chart of the runoff in rain 1.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you pour pretend rain on three small patches of ground and measure what runs off. You find out what leaves and soil do for the rain.

setup.art: Plate A with a fingertip-thick layer of soil, plate B with the same soil under a loose layer of crushed leaves, and plate C with crushed leaves only.
setup.caption: 1. Plate A: soil only. Plate B: soil with crushed leaves on top. Plate C: crushed leaves only.

setup.art: A plate with one edge resting on a stack of books and a clear glass under the lower edge, with a folded paper chute guiding water into the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one edge of the plate on books. Put a glass under the low edge, with a paper chute.

setup.art: A hand holding a tea strainer 10 centimetres above the plate while a tumbler pours water through it in a gentle shower.
setup.caption: 3. Pour 200 millilitres through the strainer, slowly, over 30 seconds.

setup.art: Two glasses side by side in front of white paper, one with muddy brown water and one with nearly clear water.
setup.caption: 4. Hold white paper behind the glasses and compare how muddy the water is.

setup.art: A child measuring water from a glass into a measuring jug, with a results table and a bar chart in a notebook.
setup.caption: 5. Measure the runoff from each plate and draw a bar for each.

flow.do: Set out three identical plates, a tea strainer, a tumbler of soil and a bowl of crushed dry leaves. Show your child what goes on each plate. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will pour pretend rain on three plates. Plate A will have only soil. Plate B will have soil with dry leaves on top. Plate C will have dry leaves and no soil. Which plate will send off the most water? Which will send off the muddiest water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Plate A has soil. Plate B has soil and leaves. Plate C has only leaves. Which sends off the muddiest water? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think that plate will send off the most water?
good: Bare soil has nothing to stop the water.
Leaves will slow the water down.
Soil soaks up water like a sponge.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the results table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Forest Floor Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Crumble the soil and spread one tumbler of it on plate A, about as thick as a fingertip. Do the same on plate B. Spread one handful of crushed leaves loosely over plate B. Spread another handful, with no soil, on plate C.
flow.say: Plate A is soil only. Plate B is the same soil with a loose blanket of crushed leaves on top. Plate C is the same leaves with no soil underneath. Only one thing changes at a time.
flow.kid: Spread soil on plates A and B. Crush the leaves into small bits. Put a handful on plate B. Put a handful on plate C.
flow.parent: Crush the leaves to pieces about the size of a postage stamp, and keep them loose. Whole leaves laid flat can act like roof tiles and send the water off. If you have no dry leaves, use dried used tea leaves. Do not press the soil down hard. If the soil slides down the tilted plate in one lump, spread it thinner and tap it flat with the back of a spoon, the same on plates A and B.

check.q: Why do we keep one plate with soil only?
options: It is the starting point to compare with
Soil is the only thing that holds water
check.why: Plate A is the starting point. Plate B differs from A in one way only, the leaves on top. So any difference between A and B comes from the leaves. Saying that soil is the only thing that holds water is a guess, and the test can check it.

flow.context: In this step, you build the three plates. Each has a different mix of soil and leaves, so you can compare them.

flow.do: Lift one edge of plate A on the stack of books. Put a labelled glass under the other edge, with a paper chute. Hold the strainer 10 centimetres above the plate. Pour 200 millilitres slowly over 30 seconds, moving the strainer back and forth. Count the seconds until the first drop reaches the glass. Repeat for plates B and C, one at a time, each with its own glass. Measure each glass and write it in the table.
flow.say: We pour 200 millilitres of pretend rain, slowly, over 30 seconds. Watch what the water does. Count the seconds before the first drop falls into the glass. Then wait two minutes for the dripping to stop, and measure.
flow.kid: Pour 200 millilitres slowly through the strainer. Count the seconds until the first drop. Wait two minutes. Measure the water in the glass.

ask.q: What do you see the water doing on each plate?
good: On plate A the water runs off fast and is brown.
On plate B the water seems to disappear into the leaves.
On plate C the water slides off the leaves.

flow.parent: Pour the same way each time, at the same height, with the plate at the same slope. If water pools behind the rim instead of flowing out, tilt the plate a little more. Write what you see even if it surprises you. On plate A the water often arrives first and is brown. On plate B it often arrives later and is clearer. If the soil is very dry and the water beads up and rolls off every plate, sprinkle a spoon of water on plates A and B and wait five minutes before you start, the same on both. Numbers differ from home to home, so compare your own three plates, not other people's. Two to four children: one pours, one times the seconds to the first drop, one holds the glass and the chute, one measures and writes. Swap roles for each plate. One child alone does the same jobs in order, and the parent holds the chute.

check.q: Why do we pour the same amount, from the same height, on each plate?
options: So that any difference comes from what is on the plate
check.why: If the rain changed from plate to plate, we could not tell whether the rain or the plate made the difference. A fair test changes only one thing at a time.

flow.context: In this step, you make the first pretend rain and catch what runs off each plate.

flow.do: Pour away the first glasses, or set them aside. Use a clean glass for each plate. Pour a second rain of 200 millilitres on plate A, then B, then C, in the same way. Wait two minutes after each. Measure each glass and write it in the table.
flow.say: Now it is raining a second time, on ground that is already wet. What do you think will change? Pour the same way. Measure what runs off.
flow.kid: It is raining again. Pour another 200 millilitres on each plate. Measure what runs off.

ask.q: Is the second rain different from the first? How?
good: More ran off plate A the second time.
The soil was already wet, so it soaked up less.
Plate B still held more than plate A.

flow.parent: Wet soil usually soaks up less, so more water often runs off in the second rain. Do not explain yet. Ask what they notice. If the numbers are very close for all plates, write them down. That is also a result.
flow.context: In this step, you make a second pretend rain on the same plates, which are now wet.

flow.do: Line up the glasses. Hold a sheet of white paper behind them. Look through each glass. Decide whether the water is clear, a little muddy or very muddy. Write it in the table. Leave the glasses for five minutes and look at the bottom.
flow.say: Which glass is the muddiest? Which is the clearest? Look again after five minutes. Where did the mud go?
flow.kid: Hold white paper behind each glass. Is the water clear, a little muddy or very muddy? Write it down.
flow.parent: Muddy water from plate A is the most common result. If all the glasses look the same, the soil may be too coarse. Try again with finer, drier soil.

check.q: Brown water running off bare soil is carrying something away. What is it?
options: Rain that has turned into mud
check.why: The brown colour is tiny bits of soil carried by the water. When water carries soil away like this, it is called erosion. Rain does not turn into mud, and the leaves do not dissolve.

flow.context: In this step, you compare how muddy the runoff from each plate is.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart. Put the three plates along the bottom and the runoff in rain 1 up the side. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then ask what would change if the leaves were taken off plate B.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each plate. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Plate C had leaves too. Why didn't leaves alone hold the water?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that plate B kept more water, or sent out clearer water, than plate A, and that plate C let the water run off. After they have said what they saw, explain: leaves slow the drops and the flow, soak up some water, and protect the soil from the beating of the drops. The soil below soaks up the rest. Each needs the other. In a forest, roots, worms, termites and fungi also open tunnels and bind the soil. If plate B did not do better than plate A, say so. That is also a result.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Forest Floor Test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Blanket Test: do dead leaves keep soil damp?
experiments.question: Three cups of soil sit in the sun. One is bare, one has a thin cover of leaves and one has a thick cover of leaves. Which cup stays damp the longest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which cup will dry out first, and which will stay damp longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup has the same soil, the same depth, the same amount of water and the same place in the sun. Cup A, bare soil, is the control: the plain cup that we compare the others with. Cup B and cup C differ from A in one way only: a cover of leaves. B and C differ from each other only in how thick the cover is.

materials.item: 3 identical cups or small pots about 8 centimetres tall, with no holes
about 4 tumblers of dry soil, crumbled
3 handfuls of dry leaves, crushed (dried used tea leaves will do for a thin cover; a thick cover needs real crushed leaves)
blunt wooden ice-cream sticks, 3 for each day (not sharp skewers). A dry chopstick or a dry twig, wiped clean between readings, also works
12 tablespoons (180 millilitres) of water, and a bowl for mixing
a ruler, a marker pen, a sunny balcony or window sill, and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the cups away from the edge of a sill or balcony so that they cannot fall. Mould can grow on damp leaves, so do not sniff the leaves. If your child has asthma or an allergy, an adult should check the cups. Wash your hands after touching soil or leaves.
experiments.record: Each day, write the length of the pale, dry part of the stick in the table. On day 5, draw a line graph with one line for each cup.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you cover soil in three different ways and check each day how dry it gets. You find out what a layer of leaves does for the water in soil.

setup.art: Three identical cups in a row, each filled with soil to 6 centimetres, labelled A, B and C.
setup.caption: 1. Fill each cup with soil, 6 centimetres deep. Label them A, B and C.

setup.art: A child pouring 4 tablespoons of water slowly into a cup of soil from a spoon, with the other two cups waiting.
setup.caption: 2. Mix the soil with water in a bowl until it is damp, then fill the cups.

setup.art: Cup A bare, cup B with a thin layer of crushed leaves, cup C with a thick layer, all on a sunny window sill.
setup.caption: 3. Leave A bare. Cover B with a thin layer of leaves and C with a thick layer. Put them in the sun.

setup.art: A wooden stick pulled out of a cup of soil, with a dark damp lower part and a pale dry upper part, and a ruler measuring the pale part.
setup.caption: 4. Each day, push a clean stick to the bottom, pull it out and measure the pale part.

flow.do: Show your child the three cups. Say that A will stay bare, B will get a thin cover of leaves and C will get a thick cover. Write down their guess and their reason.
flow.say: We will keep three cups of damp soil in the sun for five days. One is bare. One has a thin blanket of leaves. One has a thick blanket. Which will dry out first? Which will stay damp longest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Cup A is bare. Cup B has a few leaves. Cup C has a thick layer of leaves. Which dries out first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that cup will dry out first?
good: The sun can reach the bare soil.
Leaves keep the sun off.
A thick blanket will keep more water in.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write the guesses at the top of the results table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blanket Test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: In a bowl, mix all the soil with the 12 tablespoons of water until it is evenly damp, like a wrung-out cloth. Fill each cup with this soil to 6 centimetres. Leave cup A bare. Cover cup B with a layer of crushed leaves about 1 centimetre thick. Cover cup C with a layer about 3 centimetres thick. Put all three side by side in a sunny place. Do the first stick test.
flow.say: All three cups have the same soil, the same water and the same sun. Only the covering is different. To test how dry the soil is, we push a stick to the bottom, pull it out and measure the pale part.
flow.kid: Fill the cups with soil. Add water. Cover B a little and C a lot. Put them in the sun.
flow.parent: To do a stick test, push a clean stick straight down to the bottom of the cup. Pull it out. Damp soil makes the stick dark and dry soil leaves it pale. Measure the pale part of the stick, from the soil line down to where it turns dark, in centimetres, and write it in the table. On day 1 it should be 0 for all the cups. Use a new stick for every reading, or wipe the stick dry. Push the stick in at a new spot near the edge each day, and lift the leaves aside rather than pulling them off. For a covered cup, measure the pale part from the soil surface under the leaves. Two to four children: each child looks after one cup, or two children share a cup and take turns to push and to measure. Alone, you do all three cups. If it rains a lot or the air is very damp, put the cups where the sun reaches, and out of the rain. If all three cups still stay dark after five days, write that down. It is a result. Carry on for five more days, or move the cups to a warmer, sunnier place, and see which cup begins to pale first. Dry weather gives clearer results than monsoon days.

check.q: Why do all the cups get exactly the same water and the same sun?
options: So that only the cover is different
To make the soil grow plants
check.why: If one cup had more water or more sun, we could not tell if the cover or the water made the difference. Changing only the cover lets the cover alone explain what we see.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the three cups and take the first reading.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow at the same time.
flow.do: At the same time as yesterday, do the stick test on each cup with a clean stick. Measure the pale part. Write it in the table for day 2. Look at the soil and the leaves.
flow.say: What does the stick look like today? How much of it is pale? Which cup is drying out most?
flow.kid: Push a clean stick into each cup. Measure the pale part. Write it down.
flow.parent: Do not move the cups. After two days, the top of the bare cup is usually pale. If nothing has changed in any cup, that is a result.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Blanket Test. You check how dry each cup is.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow at the same time.
flow.do: Do the stick test on each cup. Measure the pale part. Write it in the table for day 3. Look under the thick cover.
flow.say: Is the pale part longer than yesterday? Which cup has changed most? What do you see under the leaves?
flow.kid: Push a clean stick into each cup. Measure the pale part. Look under the leaves.
flow.parent: Under the thick leaves you may see white threads of mould or a tiny insect. This is normal. Do not sniff or poke the soil.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Blanket Test. You check each cup again.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow at the same time.
flow.do: Do the stick test on each cup. Measure the pale part. Write it in the table for day 4.
flow.say: What is the pattern so far? What do you think the table will say on day 5?
flow.kid: Push a clean stick into each cup. Measure the pale part. Guess tomorrow's number.
flow.parent: This is a good moment to ask for a prediction. A pattern like 0, 1, 2, 3 suggests 4 for the next day.
flow.context: This is day 4 of the Blanket Test. You check each cup and guess what comes next.

flow.do: Do the last stick test. Draw a line graph. Put the days along the bottom and the pale length up the side, with one line for each cup. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each cup. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: If the thick cover kept the soil damp, would a plant grow better under it? How could you test that?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the bare cup dried fastest, and that the thicker cover slowed the drying more. After they have said what they saw, explain: sun and wind turn the water in soil into vapour. Leaves shade the soil, keep the wind off and keep it cooler, so less water escapes. This is why farmers use mulch. If the bare cup did not dry fastest, say so, and look for what else was different between the cups.

check.q: A farmer spreads straw around young vegetable plants in summer. Why?
options: The straw slows the loss of water from the soil
The straw gives the plants rain
check.why: The straw works like the leaves in the cups. It shades the soil and keeps the wind off, so the water stays in the soil for longer. Straw does not make rain or sunlight.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Blanket Test. You draw the graph and explain what you found.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up the three cups. Do the first stick test.
Stick test on each cup. Write the pale part in the table.
Stick test on each cup. Look under the leaves.
Stick test on each cup. Guess the number for day 5.
Last stick test. Draw the graph. Say what you found and why.

activities.title: Window Trail: a nature trail from one spot

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a window, a balcony or a terrace with some plants or sky in view
a hand lens, if you have one
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with you on a balcony or terrace. Never lean over the railing. Do not touch a wasp or bee nest, a spider or any creature you do not know.
activities.record: Write a list of at least eight living beings or signs of them. Then draw three arrows between pairs of them and write the link on each arrow.
activities.context: In this activity, you go on a nature trail without leaving your spot. You find living beings and their signs, and work out the links between them.

setup.art: A child sitting by a balcony railing with a notebook, a pencil and a hand lens, looking at a potted plant and a crow on a wire.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still in one spot with a notebook. Be quiet for ten minutes.

setup.art: A notebook page with a list of eight items, including a crow, ants on a wall, a nibbled leaf and a feather, with small sketches.
setup.caption: 2. Write down every living being and every sign of one.

setup.art: A notebook page with three pairs of drawings joined by arrows, each arrow labelled with a link.
setup.caption: 3. Draw an arrow from the one who gives to the one who gains. Write the link.

flow.do: Choose a spot with plants or sky in view, such as a window, a balcony or a terrace. A grown-up comes along. Read the trail rules aloud. Set a timer for ten minutes.
flow.say: We are going on a trail without going anywhere. The rules are simple. Stay put. Stay quiet. Touch nothing you do not know. Take your rubbish home.
flow.kid: Sit near the window. Stay still and quiet. Touch nothing you do not know.
flow.parent: In a flat you may see few animals. That is fine. Ants, a crow, a pigeon, a potted plant, a lizard on the wall and a spider's web all count.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Trail. You choose a spot and read the trail rules.

flow.do: Look, listen and smell for ten minutes. Write down at least eight things. Include signs, such as a nibbled leaf, a feather, a web or a snail trail. Draw the one you like best.
flow.say: What do you see? What do you hear? Is anything moving? Is anything chewed, dropped, built or dug? Write it all down.
flow.kid: Look and listen. Write down everything alive, and every sign of life. Draw your favourite.

ask.q: Which things on your list are living beings, and which are signs?
good: The crow is a living being. The feather is a sign.
The ants are living beings. The line on the wall is a sign.
The nibbled leaf is a sign.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child what they should find. Accept anything that they notice. Ask for a second look at a leaf or a wall corner. Two to four children: each sits at a different side of the window or balcony with their own notebook, then everyone compares lists and finds things only one child saw. If your list is short, count plants, sounds, and signs such as a feather or a web.
flow.context: In this step of the Window Trail, you look, listen and write down what you find.

flow.do: Choose three pairs from the list. For each pair, draw an arrow from the one who gives to the one who gains. Then write the link: food, shelter, making new plants, travel, clean-up or changing the place.
flow.say: Pick two things from your list. Does one of them need the other? What does she get? Draw an arrow, and name the link.
flow.kid: Pick two things. Draw an arrow from the giver to the one who gains. Name the link.

check.q: A crow sits on a wire and eats a fruit from a tree. Which link is this?
check.why: The crow takes food from the tree. If the crow also drops the seeds far away, that is travel. Shelter would need the crow to be nesting in the tree.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Window Trail. You join pairs from your list with arrows.

activities.title: One Tree, Many Lives: a census of a tree near you

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a tree near your building or in a park, if you have one nearby
a hand lens, if you have one
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: A grown-up comes with you. Do not climb the tree or shake her. Do not touch nests, hives or hairy caterpillars. Stay away from busy roads.
activities.record: Make a tally of the kinds of living beings and signs you find in five places: bark, leaves, flowers and fruit, the ground below, and the air around the tree. Then draw the tree with an arrow for each link.
activities.context: This activity is an extra, for families who have a tree nearby. You spend 25 minutes with one tree and find out how many kinds of lives and links depend on her.

setup.art: A child standing close to a neem tree trunk with a notebook, a grown-up beside them, looking at the bark through a lens.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one tree. Look at her bark, from top to bottom.

setup.art: A notebook page divided into five boxes labelled bark, leaves, flowers and fruit, ground, and air, each with tally marks and small drawings.
setup.caption: 2. Make five boxes in your notebook. Spend three minutes on each box.

setup.art: A drawing of the tree with six coloured arrows to the animals she shelters, feeds and cleans up after.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the tree with an arrow to each visitor and the link.

flow.do: A grown-up comes along. Choose one tree, such as a neem, a mango, a gulmohar or a peepal. Make five boxes in the notebook. Write a title on each: bark, leaves, flowers and fruit, ground, and air.
flow.say: We will spend three minutes on each part of this tree. We are counting how many kinds of living beings we find, not how many of each kind. Do not touch what you do not know.
flow.kid: Pick a tree. Draw five boxes. Name each one.
flow.parent: A road tree in a city counts. Choose one you can reach without crossing a busy road.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Tree, Many Lives. You choose a tree and prepare the notebook.

flow.do: Spend three minutes on each of the five boxes: bark, leaves, flowers and fruit, ground, and air. Make a mark or a drawing for every kind you find.
flow.say: What is on the bark? What is on the leaves? Who visits the flowers or fruit? What lies on the ground? What flies near her?
flow.kid: Look at each part of the tree for three minutes. Draw each kind you find in its box.

ask.q: Which part of the tree had the most different visitors?
good: The flowers or the fruit.
The bark, with ants and beetles.
The ground, with ants and fallen leaves.

flow.parent: Count kinds, not numbers. Ten ants are one kind. Accept 'a small black beetle' as a kind. If it is quiet, wait. Visitors often come after you are still for a few minutes. Two to four children: give each child one or two boxes to start, then swap and add what the others missed. One child alone does all five boxes in turn. Keep away from ants' nests and bee hives, and wash hands afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of One Tree, Many Lives, you look at each part of the tree in turn and note every kind of visitor.

flow.do: Draw the tree. Add an arrow for each visitor and write the link. Then ask your child what would be lost if the tree were cut.
flow.say: Draw an arrow for each visitor, and name the link. If this tree were cut down, who would lose something?
flow.kid: Draw the tree. Draw an arrow to each visitor. If the tree were cut down, who would lose something?
flow.think: Does the tree need any of her visitors?
flow.parent: Good answers name more than one loser: birds that nest, insects that eat the leaves, ants on the bark, the soil that the roots hold. Some visitors give back to the tree, such as the bee who carries pollen and the bird who carries seeds.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Tree, Many Lives. You draw the web around one tree.

activities.title: Ask an Elder: an old rule that looks after nature

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil, or a phone to record the answers
a grandparent, an older neighbour or an elder in the family, in person or by phone

activities.record: Write down the rule or custom, who made it, what it looks after, and whether it still works today.
activities.context: In this activity, you ask an older person about one rule that looks after nature. You think about how old rules and the science in this unit fit together.

setup.art: A child and a grandmother sitting together on a verandah, with a notebook and a cup of tea between them.
setup.caption: 1. Choose an elder to ask. Prepare three questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with the headings Rule, Who made it, What it looks after, Does it still work, filled in with short notes.
setup.caption: 2. Write down the rule, who made it, and what it looks after.

setup.art: A drawing of a neem leaf in a grain tin with an arrow to a small insect and a note saying keeps pests away.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the rule and the link it shows.

flow.do: Choose an elder to ask. Write three questions with your child. Include this one: 'What is one rule about trees, water, animals or food that you grew up with, and who made it?'
flow.say: We will ask about a rule that looks after nature. Many families have one. Think of a rule about a tree, a pond, a bird or food. What would you like to ask?
flow.kid: Pick an elder. Write three questions about a rule that looks after nature.
flow.parent: Examples to prompt the elder: neem leaves in the grain tin, a tulsi plant by the door, not picking leaves at night, leaving some fruit for the birds, not cutting a peepal or a banyan, a village pond that nobody washes in, thanking cattle at Pongal. Every family has different ones. Accept whatever they tell you.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask an Elder. You plan three questions.

flow.do: Ask the questions. Write down or record the answers. Ask what the rule protects, who made it, and whether people still keep it.
flow.say: What was the rule? Who taught it to you? What do you think it looks after? Do people still keep it today?
flow.kid: Ask your three questions. Write down what you hear.

ask.q: What does the rule look after?
good: A tree, a pond or an animal.
The soil or the water.
Food for the next season.

flow.parent: Listen without correcting. Some rules are about belief, and some are about practice. Both are worth hearing. Several children can ask the same elder together, taking turns with the three questions, or each ask a different elder and bring the answers back to compare. If no elder is near, a neighbour, a teacher or a relative on a phone call will do.
flow.context: In this step of Ask an Elder, you ask your questions and write down the answers.

flow.do: Draw the rule and what it looks after. Ask: does it take only what grows back? Does it keep a link in the web, such as shelter, clean-up or food? Does science tell us why it works?
flow.say: Does this rule take only what grows back? Which link does it protect? Is there a reason that science can see?
flow.kid: Draw the rule. Does it take only what grows back? Which link does it protect?

check.q: A family puts dried neem leaves in the grain tin to keep insects out. What is the best way to test whether this works?
options: Store grain with and without neem leaves, and compare
check.why: A fair test compares two tins that are the same except for the neem leaves. Asking more people tells us what people believe, not what happens in the tin. Hoping is not a test.

flow.think: Can an old rule be good even if the old reason is not the one that science would give?
flow.parent: Good answers see a plain link, such as neem leaves keeping insects out. Some rules have a reason we do not yet know. It is fine to leave that open.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ask an Elder. You think about what the rule protects.

activities.title: The Shared Pond: how much can we take?

materials.item: a large bowl for the pond
20 dry beans or dal grains for fish, such as rajma or chana
20 more beans in a spare cup
one small cup for each player to keep their fish
paper and a pencil for each player, and a score table

activities.safety: Do not eat the beans, and do not put them in your mouth. Raw rajma is harmful to eat, and small beans can make a young child choke. Keep them away from little brothers and sisters.
activities.record: For each round, write the number of beans in the pond at the start, the number each player took, the number left and the number added. Add up each player's score at the end.
activities.context: In this activity, you play a game about a shared pond whose fish grow back by a rule. You find out how much a village can take without emptying it.

setup.art: A big bowl with twenty beans in it, a spare cup with twenty more beans, and two small cups for the players, on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put 20 beans in the bowl. Keep 20 more in the spare cup.

setup.art: Two players each writing a number secretly on a slip of paper, then revealing them together.
setup.caption: 2. Each player secretly writes a number from 0 to 5. Show them together.

setup.art: A hand adding beans from the spare cup to the bowl, with a note saying for every 2 left, add 1.
setup.caption: 3. Take your beans. Count the beans left. For every 2 left, add 1 from the spare cup.

flow.do: Put 20 beans in the bowl. The bowl is the pond and each bean is a fish. Keep 20 beans in the spare cup. Read the rules. Each round, every player secretly writes a number from 0 to 5. Everyone shows their number at the same time and takes that many beans. Then count what is left. For every 2 beans left, add 1 from the spare cup. The pond never holds more than 20. Each bean you take is 1 point. If the players ask for more beans than the pond holds, they take in turn until it is empty. A pond with only 1 bean left adds none.
flow.say: This is our village pond. Each round, each of us secretly writes how many fish to take, from 0 to 5. Then the pond grows back by a rule. For every 2 fish left, 1 new fish is born. Play eight rounds, or until the pond is empty.
flow.kid: The bowl is a pond. Each bean is a fish. Write 0 to 5. Take your fish. Count what is left.
flow.parent: Playing alone: play against the Village. The Village takes 4 beans every round. You choose how many to take. In game 2, the Village takes only 2 beans every round. Two or three players: each writes 0 to 5. Four players: each writes 0 to 3, so the pond can last. Beans are only counters, so any small dry thing works, such as pebbles or buttons, and then there is no food-safety worry. A total of about 6 taken each round is what a pond that holds 20 can bear. Do not tell the children this number. Let them find it.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Shared Pond. You set up the pond and learn the rules.

flow.do: Play game 1 with no talking. Write each round in the table. Stop after eight rounds, or when the pond is empty. Add up each player's score.
flow.say: This is game 1, and there is no talking. Write your number. Show it. Take your fish. Count what is left, and add the new fish.
flow.kid: Write your number. Show it. Take your fish. Add new fish. Write it down.

check.q: After everyone has taken, 6 beans are left. How many are added?
check.why: For every 2 beans left, 1 is added. 6 beans is 3 groups of 2, so 3 beans are added. The pond then holds 9 beans.

flow.context: In this step of The Shared Pond, you play the first game with no talking.

flow.do: Reset the pond to 20 beans. Before you play, talk for two minutes and agree on a rule. Write it down. Play eight rounds again. Keep each other to the rule.
flow.say: Game 2. This time we may talk first. What rule would keep the pond full and still give each of us fish? Let's write it down and keep it.
flow.kid: Reset the pond. Talk first. Make a rule. Play again and keep to the rule.

ask.q: What happened to the pond when you made a rule together?
good: It stayed full.
We all got more fish in the end.
We watched each other.

flow.parent: In game 1, a pond usually empties by round 5 or 6 if players take 4 or 5 each. If the total taken in one round is 6 or less, the pond usually refills. Let your child find the number.
flow.context: In this step of The Shared Pond, you talk first and make a rule, then play again.

flow.do: Compare the scores of the two games. Ask: which game gave more fish to everyone in the end, and why?
flow.say: Which game gave us more fish in total? What was the rule that worked? Who should decide the rule for a real village pond?
flow.kid: Compare your two scores. Which game was better? Why?
flow.think: If the pond could take 6 fish a round, how should we share the 6?
flow.parent: Sharing the 6 fairly is a real puzzle. Some villages share equally, some by need, some by turns. There is no single right answer. Ask your child why they chose theirs.
flow.context: This is the last step of The Shared Pond. You compare the two games and think about fairness.

projects.title: Grow a Root Mat: do living roots hold soil?

materials.item: 2 large plates, the same kind as in the Forest Floor Test (one for the root mat, one bare to compare)
2 tumblers (400 millilitres) of the same dry soil as in the Forest Floor Test
2 tablespoons of methi (fenugreek) seeds
a tea strainer, a measuring jug marked at 200 millilitres, 2 clear glasses, a stack of books 5 centimetres high, and a folded paper chute
your results table from the Forest Floor Test (for comparison only)

schedule.what: Spread soil on two plates. Scatter the methi seeds on one. Sprinkle both with water.
Sprinkle a little water so the soil stays damp. Look for sprouts.
Sprinkle a little water. Measure the tallest sprout.
Sprinkle a little water. Draw what you see.
Sprinkle a little water. Look at the roots at the edge of the plate.
Sprinkle a little water. Stop watering after today.
Pour the pretend rain on the root mat plate and on the bare plate. Compare them. Explain what you see.

projects.safety: Do not eat the seeds or the sprouts from this plate, because the soil is not clean. Wash your hands after touching soil. Keep the plate away from the edge of a sill. Methi can upset a child who is allergic to it, so an adult decides if your child should handle it. Wash your hands after the rain test.
projects.record: Draw the root mat plate on day 1 and on day 7. For both plates, write the seconds to the first drop, the millilitres that ran off and how muddy the water was.
projects.context: In this project, you grow a thin green mat of methi on a plate of soil for a week. Then you pour the same pretend rain on it as in the Forest Floor Test. You find out if living roots hold soil.

setup.art: A plate with a fingertip layer of soil, and a child scattering small fenugreek seeds over it with a spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Spread soil on the plate. Scatter the seeds. Press them in.

setup.art: The same plate on day 5 with a thin carpet of green sprouts, with a ruler beside the tallest one.
setup.caption: 2. Water a little each day. Watch the green mat grow.

setup.art: The root mat plate tilted on books with a glass under the low edge and a strainer pouring rain, next to the bare plate A.
setup.caption: 3. On day 7, pour the same rain as before and compare with plate A.

flow.do: Soak the methi seeds in water overnight if you can. Spread one tumbler of soil on each plate, about as thick as a fingertip. On plate 1, scatter the methi seeds evenly and press them in lightly. Leave plate 2 bare, as the comparison. Sprinkle both plates with the same amount of water until the soil is damp. Put both in the same light place.
flow.say: Today we plant a mat of tiny plants on a plate of soil. In a week we will pour pretend rain on it, the same rain as in the Forest Floor Test. What do you think the roots will do?
flow.kid: Spread soil. Scatter seeds. Sprinkle water. Put the plate in the light.

ask.q: What do you think will happen when rain falls on a plate full of roots?
good: The roots will hold the soil.
Less mud will wash away.
The water will soak in.

flow.parent: Do not eat the seeds or the sprouts from this plate, because the soil is not clean. Keep the soil damp, not soaked. If your home is cold, put the plate near a window. Two to four children: each pair of children grows their own pair of plates, or one pair of plates is shared and the children take turns to water and to measure. Methi usually sprouts in two to three days in warm weather, and may take longer in the cold.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Root Mat. You plant the seeds on a plate of soil.

flow.wait: Come back each day, from day 2 to day 6.
flow.do: Sprinkle the same small amount of water on both plates. Look at the sprouts. On one day, measure the tallest one with a ruler. On another day, draw what you see.
flow.say: What has changed since yesterday? Are the roots visible at the edge of the plate?
flow.kid: Sprinkle a little water. Look at the sprouts. Draw or measure them.
flow.parent: Water for the last time on day 6, so the soil is damp but not wet on day 7.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 6 of the Root Mat. You water the plate and watch it grow.

flow.do: Tilt plate 1, the root mat, on the books. Put a glass under the low edge, with a chute of foil or thin plastic. Pour 200 millilitres through the strainer over 30 seconds. Note the seconds to the first drop. Measure the runoff and look at the colour. Then do exactly the same with the bare plate 2. Compare the two.
flow.say: This is the same rain, on the same slope, on two plates that were watered the same. Only one has roots. Count the seconds to the first drop. Then we measure what runs off and look at the colour.
flow.kid: Tilt the plate. Pour rain slowly on the mat, then on the bare plate. Count seconds. Measure the runoff. Look at the colour.

ask.q: How is the runoff from the root mat different from the runoff from the bare plate?
good: There is less mud.
It took longer for the first drop.
There is less water.

flow.parent: The water from the root mat is often clearer than the water from the bare plate, but not always. The numbers will also differ from your Forest Floor Test numbers, because this soil is damp. So compare plate 1 with plate 2, not with the Forest Floor Test table. If the sprouts are patchy, that is a result too. A thin mat still holds more soil than none.

check.q: What do the roots of a plant do for the soil on a slope?
options: They grip the soil and make tunnels for water
They only take water from it
check.why: Roots hold soil crumbs together and open tunnels, so water sinks in. They do take water too, but they also hold the slope in place. Saying they have no effect does not match what you saw.

flow.context: This is day 7 of the Root Mat. You pour the same pretend rain as in the Forest Floor Test and compare the two plates.

flow.do: Put your Root Mat numbers next to your bare plate numbers. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Ask what a hillside with no plants would lose in a heavy monsoon.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Compare the mat with the bare plate. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A bare hillside has no roots. What would the monsoon do to it?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the roots held the soil, so the water was clearer, and that the plants also shaded the soil. After they have said it, explain: roots and fine root hairs grip soil crumbs, and the tunnels they leave let water sink in. This is why hill farmers plant grass and trees on slopes.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Root Mat. You compare and explain.

challenges.title: Slow the Rain: stop a slope from washing away
challenges.problem: A path across a school hillside turns into a muddy stream every monsoon, and the soil ends up in the road. Your plate of soil is a model of that slope. Make the rain run off slower and clearer, using only things from home.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Use the same plate, the same amount of soil, the same slope and the same 200 millilitres of rain as in the Forest Floor Test.
Do not use glue, tape or anything you cannot throw in the compost afterwards.
Test each idea on its own plate, so you can compare.
materials: a plate with a fingertip layer of soil, one for each idea
dry leaves, straw, coconut coir or a piece of old cloth
twigs, ice-cream sticks or rolled-up strips of cloth
a tea strainer and a measuring jug
clear glasses, books, paper chutes and white paper
general: Cover the soil with a layer of dry leaves, like a forest floor.
Cover the soil with a piece of cloth or a jute sack.
Spread straw or coconut coir over the soil.
creative: Shape the soil into small ridges across the slope, like steps, so the water stops and sinks in at each step.
Lay rolled-up strips of cloth or a line of twigs across the slope, so that they catch mud as it moves.
Leave a strip of thick leaves along the low edge as a filter, and keep the upper part bare.
challenges.your_turn: Test two of your own ideas on two plates, with the same rain on each. Measure the runoff and look at the mud. Choose the best, and say why. Then say how it could work on a real hillside.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about rain and soil. You design a way to keep a slope from washing away, and test it with the same pretend rain as in the Forest Floor Test.

setup.art: Three plates with soil on a table: one covered with leaves, one with ridges across the slope, one with a line of twigs.
setup.caption: 1. Make a different cover or shape on each plate.

setup.art: A plate tilted on books with a strainer pouring rain and a glass catching the runoff.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the same rain on each plate and catch what runs off.

setup.art: Three glasses in front of white paper showing muddy, a little muddy and clear water.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the glasses. Choose the best idea.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about what makes soil wash away. Ask for two ideas for slowing the rain.
flow.say: In the Forest Floor Test, leaves helped. What else might slow the rain down on a slope? Think of things from home.
flow.kid: Rain washes soil away. How can you slow it down? Think of two ideas.

ask.q: What stops a stream of water from running fast?
good: A wall or a ridge across it.
Something rough or soft.
A place for it to sink in.

flow.context: This is the first step of Slow the Rain. You think about the problem.

flow.do: Build two ideas on two plates, one idea on each. Use the same soil and the same slope. Pour 200 millilitres of rain on each, as in the Forest Floor Test. Catch the runoff in a glass.
flow.say: Build one idea on each plate. Make a guess about which will work better, and why. Then pour the same rain.
flow.kid: Build one idea on each plate. Pour the same rain. Catch the runoff.
flow.parent: Let your child decide. Do not suggest an answer. If an idea fails, that is useful information.
flow.context: In this step of Slow the Rain, you build and test two ideas.

flow.do: Measure the runoff from each plate. Look at the colour against white paper. Write the numbers. Which idea was best? Which was worst?
flow.say: Which glass is the clearest? Which has the least water? What does that tell us about your ideas?
flow.kid: Measure the runoff. Look at the colour. Which idea is best?

check.q: Idea A gave less runoff than idea B, but muddier water. Which idea is better at keeping the soil on the slope?
check.why: Muddy water means soil is leaving the slope. Idea B gave more runoff but clearer water, so it kept more soil. A good design has to be judged on both the water and the mud.

flow.context: In this step of Slow the Rain, you measure and compare your two ideas.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why the best idea worked. Then show a picture of terraces or vetiver grass rows on a hillside. Ask how the idea would work on a real hill.
flow.say: Why did the best idea work? What would you do on a real hillside? Farmers in India dig terraces and plant rows of vetiver grass. How are those like your idea?
flow.kid: Why did your best idea work? How would it work on a real hill?
flow.think: Which of your ideas could a village build with its own hands?
flow.parent: Good answers link the idea to the forest floor: slow the water, give it a place to sink in, hold the soil. Terraces make flat steps that stop the flow. Vetiver grass has deep roots that grip the soil.
