worksheets.title: The Forest Floor and the Web (core)

items.p: What is leaf litter?
opts: The layer of fallen leaves, twigs and fruits on the ground
Leaves that are still on the tree
Rubbish left behind by visitors
items.why: Leaf litter is the natural carpet of dead leaves, twigs, flowers and fruits on the ground. It is not rubbish. It soaks up rain, keeps the soil damp and feeds worms and fungi.

items.p: Rain water that flows over the top of the ground, instead of soaking in, is called what?
opts: Runoff
Infiltration
Evaporation
items.why: Runoff flows over the surface. Infiltration is water soaking down into the ground. Evaporation is water turning into vapour and rising into the air.

items.p: Why does a layer of leaves keep soil damp for longer?
opts: It shades the soil and keeps the wind off, so less water escapes
It adds water to the soil
It stops the sun from ever reaching the soil
items.why: Sun and wind turn the water in soil into vapour. Leaves shade the soil and keep the wind away, so less water leaves. The leaves do not add water, and some warmth still gets through.

items.p: Which one shows the link called travel?
opts: A bird's dropping with seeds that sprout far from the tree
A bee drinking nectar
A termite eating dead wood
items.why: In travel, an animal carries a plant's seeds to a new place. A bee at a flower shows making new plants, and a termite eating dead wood shows clean-up.

items.p: A friend says: 'The web of life is just who eats whom.' What would you say?
opts: There are other links too, such as shelter, travel, clean-up and changing the place
Yes, eating is the only link
Links only matter in a forest
items.why: Eating is one link. A bird nesting in a tree, a worm opening the soil and a bee carrying pollen are links too. Saying eating is the only one misses most of the web.

items.p: Bare soil on a slope loses more soil in heavy rain than soil covered with leaf litter.
items.why: True. Raindrops break the crumbs of bare soil and the water carries the mud away. Leaf litter breaks the fall of the drops and slows the water, so less soil is lost.

items.p: A termite tunnel can help rain water sink into the ground.
items.why: True. Termite tunnels are small channels that carry water down into the soil. This is why termites are called ecosystem engineers.

items.p: Spreading leaves, straw or husk over soil to keep it damp is called ____.
items.why: Mulch is a layer that covers the soil. It shades the soil and keeps the wind off, so water stays in the soil longer.

items.p: When water carries soil away from a slope, this is called ____.
items.why: Erosion is soil being carried away by water or wind. It makes hillsides thin and fills rivers and ponds with mud.

items.p: Match each sign to the link it shows most clearly.
pairs: A dropping full of fig seeds
Travel
A thin mud tube up a tree trunk
Clean-up
A hole in a tree with a bird flying in and out
Shelter
Bees buzzing at a flowering tree
Making new plants
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A dropping with seeds carries seeds away, so it shows travel. Termites in a mud tube eat dead wood, which is clean-up. A nesting hole shows shelter. Bees carrying pollen help the tree make seeds, which is making new plants.

items.p: Sort each example by whether it keeps water in the ground or lets it run off.
items: leaf litter on a forest floor
bare, swept soil on a steep slope
coconut husk round a banana plant
a thick mat of grass roots
a cleared hillside with no plants
items.a: as given
items.why: Litter, husk and roots slow the water and open the soil, so water sinks in. Pavement and bare steep slopes have nothing to slow it, so the water runs off.

items.p: Put these in order for what happens when rain falls on a forest.
a: Rain lands on the leaves of the trees
The leaf litter soaks up some water and slows the rest
The water sinks down through root and worm tunnels
The soil holds the water in its tiny gaps
The water seeps out slowly into a spring
items.why: The rain meets the leaves first, then the litter, then the tunnels and the soil. The soil lets it go slowly into springs, which is why streams can keep flowing in the dry months.

items.p: A friend says: 'Plate C had leaves, so it should hold the most water.' What would you tell your friend, using what you saw in the Forest Floor Test?
items.a: Leaves with no soil underneath let the water slide off the hard plate. The soil with leaves on top kept more of the water and let out clearer water. The holding comes from soil and leaves working together, not from leaves alone.
items.why: A strong answer says that plate C let the water run off, and that the soil and the leaves together did better. It names both parts.

items.p: Why do farmers spread straw around young vegetable plants in summer? Use what you saw in the Blanket Test.
items.a: The straw shades the soil and keeps the wind off it, so less water turns into vapour. The soil stays damp for longer, like the cups with leaves in the Blanket Test.
items.why: A strong answer links the straw to less evaporation and damper soil, using the cups as evidence.

items.p: Draw a cross-section of a forest floor. Show leaf litter, soil, a root, a worm tunnel and rain sinking in.
items.a: A layer of leaves on top, soil below, a root going down, a tunnel for a worm, and arrows showing water going down through the litter and the tunnels.
items.why: A strong drawing shows rain meeting the litter first, then going down through the tunnels. It shows that the water is held in the soil, not only on the surface.

items.p: Plate A let 90 millilitres run off from 200 millilitres of pretend rain. How much of the rain stayed in the soil?
items.why: 200 take away 90 is 110. So 110 millilitres soaked in. A smaller runoff means more water was held.

items.p: Termites dig tunnels that let rain sink in, and later snakes use the old mounds as homes. What do we call beings who change a place like this?
opts: Ecosystem engineers
Scavengers
Pollinators
items.why: An ecosystem engineer changes a place so much that it becomes a home for others. Scavengers eat dead animals and pollinators carry pollen.

items.p: Which fishing rule is sustainable?
opts: A ban on fishing in the breeding season
Taking every fish that is breeding
Fishing only at night
items.why: A ban in the breeding season leaves fish to lay eggs, so the stock refills. Taking every breeding fish empties the water, and the time of day does not change how many fish are left.

items.p: How could you best find out whether sacred groves hold more kinds of plants than the forests next to them?
opts: Count the kinds of plants in patches of the same size in both
Ask which one is older
Look at a photograph of each
items.why: A fair comparison counts the same-sized patches in both places. Age and photographs do not measure the number of kinds.

items.p: In the Forest Floor Test, why do we pour rain a second time as well as a first time?
opts: Wet soil can behave differently from dry soil
Two numbers always look better
To use up the water
items.why: Soil that is already wet soaks up less, so more water runs off in the second rain. This is how floods can follow days of heavy rain.

items.p: A forest with no soil animals or fungi would still be a perfect sponge, because the leaves do all the work.
items.why: False. The tunnels, threads and crumbs that hold water are made by roots, worms, termites and fungi. Without them, the soil is more like dust.

items.p: If every family in a village takes a little more than their share from the pond, the pond can still last for ever.
items.why: False. If the total taken is more than the pond can grow back, the pond shrinks until it is empty. Each family's small extra adds up.

items.p: A plant lets water go as vapour through tiny holes in her leaves. This is called ____.
items.why: Transpiration sends large amounts of water from the soil into the air. Part of this water falls again as rain somewhere downwind.

items.p: Match each person to what they showed.
pairs: Charles Darwin
earthworms bring up many tonnes of soil a year
Elinor Ostrom
villages can keep shared things safe with their own rules
Garrett Hardin
a shared field can be ruined when each person takes a little more
Gaura Devi and the women of Reni
ordinary people can stop trees being cut
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Darwin weighed the soil that worms bring up. Hardin described a danger for shared things, and Ostrom showed many villages avoided it. The women of Reni stood in front of trees and the contractors left.

items.p: Eight farmers share a canal that runs for 96 minutes each morning. How many minutes does each farmer get? If 4 more farmers join, how many minutes does each get?
items.a: 12 minutes, then 8 minutes
items.why: 96 divided by 8 is 12. With 4 more farmers there are 12 farmers, and 96 divided by 12 is 8. More people sharing the same water means a smaller share for each.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Termite, earthworm, tree root, rain cloud.
items.a: The rain cloud, because the other three are living beings that change the soil.
items.why: Termites, worms and roots all open and hold the soil. A rain cloud is not a living being and does not shape the soil from within.

items.p: Sort each example by the link it shows most.
items: a spider with a fly in her web
a crow's nest in a tree
a seed in a bird's dropping
items.a: as given
items.why: Eating shows food. A nest shows shelter. Seeds carried away show travel. Beetles and fungi that break down dead wood show clean-up.

items.p: A hill village has a sacred grove at the top. A road company wants to cut a path through its edge.

views.says: The grove has been kept whole for generations. If one edge is cut, the rule is broken for everyone.
The path will save children an hour's walk to school. Only a thin strip of trees is needed.
A path can let in wind, light and cattle, and dry out the grove from the edge. We should check where else the road could go, and what the grove's streams need.

items.ask: Whose reasons are strongest, and what would you want to find out before deciding?
items.a: Answers vary. A good answer takes at least two views seriously and asks for evidence, such as other routes or the effect on water.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses the idea of a web, where an edge affects the inside, and also takes the children's need seriously.

items.p: A village pond is shrinking. Some say each family should be given a fixed number of buckets a day. Others say it should stay free for everyone.

views.who: Garrett Hardin, in an imagined version of his view
views.says: If it is free for everyone, each family will take more, and the pond will empty. We need an owner or a government to ration it.

views.who: Elinor Ostrom, in an imagined version of her view
views.says: Villagers know their pond best. If they make the rules together and watch each other, they can keep it safe.

items.ask: Which view fits what happened in your Shared Pond game, and why?
items.a: Answers vary. A good answer refers to the two games. Usually the pond emptied in the game with no talking, and lasted in the game with a shared rule.
items.why: Both views have evidence. A strong answer says that rules matter, and that the people who use the pond are often the best ones to make and keep them.

items.p: In your own words, explain why a forest floor can hold water even though no leaf, root or worm can do it alone.
items.a: Leaves slow the rain and soak up some water. Roots, worms and termites make tunnels so that water sinks in. Fungi and roots hold the soil crumbs together, and the soil holds water in its tiny gaps. Take one part away and the holding gets worse, so it belongs to all of them together.
items.why: A strong answer names at least three parts, says what each does, and says the holding comes from them working together.

items.p: A friend says: 'Sacred groves are only superstition.' Using what you know, what would you say?
items.a: Many groves hold old trees and plants that are rare outside, and some protect springs. The rule of taking nothing has kept them safe for centuries. Scientists still ask how much groves protect, and many are shrinking, so the rule alone does not save everything.
items.why: A strong answer separates the belief from the effect, gives evidence that groves protect nature, and is honest about what is still debated.

items.p: Draw the pond in the Shared Pond game over four rounds, when the villagers take too much. Show how the number of fish changes.
items.a: Four ponds in a row with fewer and fewer fish, such as 20, 10, 5 and then none, with arrows showing the villagers taking fish and a few new fish being born.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the pond shrinking each round, because more is taken than grows back.

items.p: Three cups of soil are left for four days. P is bare and in the sun. Q is in the sun with a thin cover of leaves. R is bare but in the shade. After four days P is driest, and Q and R are both damper. What does this best show?
opts: Shade and a cover of leaves both reduce drying
Only shade matters
Leaves make no difference
items.why: Both Q and R lost less water than P. Q had leaves and R had shade, so both reduce the drying. Saying leaves make no difference does not match Q.

items.p: The same rain is poured on two plates. Plate X has a mat of grass roots and plate Y is bare soil. The water from Y is brown and arrives in 5 seconds. The water from X is clear and arrives after 40 seconds. What does this suggest?
opts: Roots hold the soil and let water sink in
Plate X got less rain
Plate Y has more soil
items.why: Plate X's water arrived later and was clearer, so the roots slowed the water and held the soil. The rain was the same, so plate X did not get less.

items.p: A city covers every yard with concrete and sends the rain into drains. After a big rain the streets flood. Which idea from this unit explains this best?
opts: Concrete stops water sinking in, so all of it runs off
Concrete makes the rain heavier
Drains make more rain
items.why: Concrete has no tunnels or roots, so there is no infiltration and all the rain runs off at once. Concrete does not change how much rain falls.

items.p: Which sentence is best supported by the Forest Floor Test?
opts: Holding water is done by soil and leaves working together
The biggest tree holds most of the water
Soil alone holds all of the water
items.why: The plate with soil and leaves did better than the plate with soil alone and the plate with leaves alone. The test used no tree at all.

items.p: All scientists agree that big forests pull wet air in from the sea.
items.why: False. Many agree that plants send water into the air and that this becomes part of the rain. Whether forests also pull in sea air, the biotic pump idea, is still debated.

items.p: One player taking less from a shared pond can always save it, however much the others take.
items.why: False. What matters is the total taken each round. If the others take more than the pond can grow back, one player's restraint cannot save it alone.

items.p: A being who changes a place so much that others can or cannot live there is called an ecosystem ____.
items.why: Termites, earthworms, roots and elephants that dig waterholes are ecosystem engineers.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Runoff
water flowing over the top of the ground
Infiltration
water soaking down into the soil
Erosion
soil being carried away
Mulch
a layer of leaves or straw spread over soil
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Runoff flows on top. Infiltration goes down. Erosion is what runoff can do to soil. Mulch is a cover that slows both runoff and drying.

items.p: In the Forest Floor Test, plate B let 50 millilitres run off in rain 1 and 80 millilitres in rain 2. How much more ran off in rain 2? What fraction of the 200 millilitres ran off in rain 2, in its simplest form?
items.a: 30 millilitres more, and 2 fifths
items.why: 80 take away 50 is 30. 80 out of 200 is 80 over 200. Dividing top and bottom by 40 gives 2 over 5.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A kavu, cutting only the oldest bamboo stems, a fishing ban in the breeding season, a trawler that takes every fish.
items.a: The trawler that takes every fish, because the others protect a place or take only what grows back.
items.why: A grove, careful bamboo cutting and a breeding ban all leave enough for the future. A trawler that takes every fish leaves too little to breed.

items.p: Sort each action by whether it is sustainable if done year after year.
items: burning all fallen leaves and leaving a steep slope bare
building a johad to hold monsoon rain
pumping a well dry every summer with nothing to refill it
items.a: as given
items.why: Sustainable actions leave enough to renew. Catching every breeding fish, leaving a slope bare and pumping a well dry use something up faster than it returns.

items.p: A school wants to sweep away the dead leaves under its big trees every day, to keep the ground neat.

views.says: Leaves make the ground look untidy, and children can slip on wet ones.
Leaves keep the soil damp and feed the worms. Bare ground under the trees dries out and washes away.
We could keep a leaf patch in one corner, away from the paths, and sweep only the paths.

items.ask: Which idea do you prefer, and what evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A good answer uses the Blanket Test and the Forest Floor Test as evidence, and notices the safety point.
items.why: A strong answer takes the safety reason seriously and finds a way to keep the benefits of the leaves, as the child's idea does.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether leaf litter helps grass seeds sprout. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would measure.
items.a: Plant the same number of grass seeds in two cups of the same soil. Cover one with leaves and leave the other bare. Give the same water and keep them in the same place. After a week, count how many seeds sprouted in each cup.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, the leaf cover, keeps everything else the same, and measures the number of sprouts. It includes a bare cup as the control.

items.p: Elinor Ostrom found villages that kept shared forests and canals safe for hundreds of years. Why might rules made by the villagers work better than rules made far away?
items.a: The villagers know the place and who uses it. They can see who takes too much and they feel the loss if the forest is spoiled. Rules they made themselves are easier to follow and to adjust.
items.why: A strong answer mentions local knowledge, being able to watch each other, and agreeing to the rules. It is honest that this does not work everywhere.

items.p: The same rain falls on a swept yard and on a leafy grove. Explain what you would see in each, using the words runoff, infiltration and erosion.
items.a: In the swept yard, most of the rain would be runoff and little would sink in. The water would carry soil away, which is erosion. In the grove, the litter and tunnels let the rain sink in, so there is more infiltration, little runoff and almost no erosion.
items.why: A strong answer uses all three words correctly and contrasts the two places.

items.p: Draw a web around one tree on your street. Show at least five links and name the kind of each.
items.a: A tree in the middle, with at least five arrows to different visitors, such as a bird, an ant, a bee, a squirrel and a termite, each labelled food, shelter, travel, making new plants or clean-up.
items.why: A strong drawing names five links of at least three different kinds, not only food.

quiz.p: Which sentence best describes a web of life?
opts: All the living beings of a place and every link between them
A spider's web in a forest
A list of who eats whom
quiz.why: A web of life is the whole set of links between the beings in one place. Eating is one link, but not the only one.

quiz.p: Which of these is a link that is not about eating?
opts: A bird nesting in a tree hole
A tiger eating a deer
A cow eating grass
quiz.why: A nest is shelter. The other two are food links.

quiz.p: In the Forest Floor Test, why is plate A, with bare soil, called the control?
opts: It is the starting point to compare the others with
It has the most soil
It is the first plate
quiz.why: The control is the plain version. Each other plate differs from it in one way, so we can see what that change does.

quiz.p: Muddy brown water running off a slope means what?
opts: Soil is being carried away, which is erosion
The rain is dirty
The slope has too many leaves
quiz.why: The brown colour is tiny bits of soil. Water carrying soil away is erosion. Leaves on a slope reduce it.

quiz.p: Which of these is an ecosystem engineer?
opts: Termites that dig tunnels and build mounds
A crow sitting on a wire
A rain cloud
quiz.why: Termites change the soil and the land so much that others can use their tunnels and mounds. A crow on a wire does not change the place.

opts: It keeps the soil damp and cool
It makes the soil as cold as ice
It adds sunlight
quiz.why: Mulch shades the soil and keeps the wind off it, so less water evaporates. It does not add sunlight.

quiz.p: A dropping full of purple seeds lies under a fig tree. Which link does it show?
opts: Travel of seeds
Clean-up
Shelter
quiz.why: The animal ate the figs and is carrying the seeds in her gut. The dropping puts them in a new place. That is travel.

quiz.p: What did Elinor Ostrom find about shared meadows, forests and canals?
opts: Many were kept safe for centuries by rules the villagers made
They were always ruined
Only governments can save them
quiz.why: She studied real villages and found many shared things that lasted for centuries. People made rules, watched each other and fined cheats.

quiz.p: A sacred grove protects only the trees in it, and has no link to water.
quiz.why: False. Many groves also feed springs and streams. Scientists are still studying how much groves protect.

quiz.p: A bamboo clump grows new stems every year. Which way of cutting is sustainable?
opts: Cutting only the oldest stems
Cutting every stem
Cutting only the youngest stems
quiz.why: Old stems can be cut while the young ones keep the clump growing. Cutting every stem kills the clump, and cutting the youngest takes away its future.

quiz.p: Which is the best reason to leave fallen leaves under a tree in a garden?
opts: They soak up rain, keep the soil damp and feed the worms
They look untidy and that is good
They stop the tree growing
quiz.why: Leaf litter protects the soil from the beating of the rain, keeps it damp and feeds the animals and fungi that make the soil.

quiz.p: What do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether a forest is best seen as one whole or as many separate lives
Whether leaves can soak up water
Whether rain falls on forests
quiz.why: Ecologists have argued about this for over a hundred years. The other two are settled by measurements.

applications: Farmers spread paddy straw, sugarcane leaves or coconut husk around crops to keep the soil damp and cool.
Hill farmers dig terraces and plant rows of vetiver grass along slopes, so rain sinks in and soil stays.
Forest departments and villages plant trees and shrubs on bare hillsides to help hold the soil on slopes.
Villages in Rajasthan build johads, small earth dams that hold monsoon rain so that it sinks into the ground and refills wells.
Gardeners and city parks leave fallen leaves under trees, because the litter keeps the soil damp and feeds the worms.
Fishing is banned for weeks every monsoon in Kerala and other states, so that fish can breed.
Community forest groups in many Indian villages make their own rules about who may collect wood, grass and fruit, and how much.
Builders and city planners leave open soil and trees around buildings, so that rain sinks in instead of flooding the street.

open_questions.q: How much do sacred groves protect the plants, animals and water around them?
open_questions.why_open: Only a small share of the thousands of groves have been studied, and each one is different, so no one can give a single answer yet.

open_questions.q: Do big forests pull wet air in from the sea, as the biotic pump idea says?
open_questions.why_open: The idea has been tested with models and rain records, but scientists disagree about how strong the effect is.

open_questions.q: What do most of the living beings in a handful of forest soil actually do?
open_questions.why_open: Most soil bacteria and fungi have never been grown in a laboratory. Scientists can read their DNA, but often cannot tell what they do.

open_questions.q: How much of the web of life has nobody noticed yet?
open_questions.why_open: About two million kinds of living beings have names. Scientists think there are millions more, mostly insects and small soil animals, and the guesses range widely.

open_questions.q: Can a community always learn to share a common thing without being forced?
open_questions.why_open: Ostrom found conditions that help, but not a recipe that works everywhere. Shared things that cross many countries, such as the air and the oceans, are much harder.

open_questions.q: Is a forest more like one body, or like many separate lives?
open_questions.why_open: The answer depends on what we mean by a body, and ecologists have not agreed for over a hundred years.

ask_kids: Where in our building or street does the rain sink into the ground, and where does it run off?
Who do you think lives under the pile of dry leaves outside, and what do they do there?
Which tree near us has the most visitors, and what do they each want from her?
Is there a place near us that nobody owns but everyone uses? Who looks after it?
If you could ask the oldest person in our family about one old rule that looks after nature, what would you ask?
What is one thing we take from nature every day, and does it grow back?
Why do you think some people will not even pick up a dead leaf from a grove?
If you were a termite, a worm or a root, what would you do for the forest today?

jokes.j: Why are forests good at keeping secrets?
jokes.a: They keep everything under wraps, and they are full of leaves.

jokes.j: Why did the bamboo clump never run out of stems?
jokes.a: She only cut back on the oldest ones.

jokes.j: What did the tree say when the monsoon finally came?
jokes.a: A drink on the house, at last.

jokes.j: Why did the termite win the digging contest?
jokes.a: She was the only one who could really tunnel through a problem.

jokes.j: Why did the fungus get invited to every forest meeting?
jokes.a: She was good at connecting everyone.

jokes.j: Which plate won the rain race?
jokes.a: The one with the leafy cover. She kept her cool.

jokes.j: What did the leaf say to the soil?
Why did the village pond need rules?

maths.problem: 200 millilitres of pretend rain is poured on each of three plates. Plate A lets 120 millilitres run off, plate B lets 60 millilitres run off, and plate C lets 160 millilitres run off. How much water did plate B hold back? How many times more water ran off plate A than plate B?
maths.answer: Plate B held back 140 millilitres. Plate A let 2 times as much run off.
maths.explain: 200 take away 60 is 140, so plate B held back 140 millilitres. 120 divided by 60 is 2, so plate A let twice as much run off as plate B.
maths.context: In the Forest Floor Test, you pour the same pretend rain on three plates and measure what runs off.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting what ran off from what was poured tells us how much each plate held back. Dividing compares two plates fairly.

maths.problem: Runoff is measured from two plates. Plate A has bare soil, and plate B has soil with leaves on top. Plate A let 80 millilitres run off in rain 1 and 130 millilitres in rain 2. Plate B let 30 millilitres run off in rain 1 and 60 millilitres in rain 2. By how much did the runoff grow on each plate? What does the bigger rise on plate A suggest about wet soil?
maths.answer: Plate A grew by 50 millilitres and plate B by 30 millilitres. Bare soil that is already wet sheds more of the next rain.
maths.explain: 130 minus 80 is 50, and 60 minus 30 is 30. Plate A's runoff rose more. Wet bare soil is already full of water and its surface is sealed with mud, so more of the second rain runs off. The leaves on plate B slowed the water, so the rise was smaller.
maths.context: In the Forest Floor Test, you pour rain twice on each plate, the second time on wetter soil.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how much each number grew helps us see which plate was changed more by the first rain, and then reason about why.

maths.problem: Plate B in the Forest Floor Test received 200 millilitres of rain, and 60 millilitres ran off. What fraction of the rain ran off, and what fraction was held back? Write each as a fraction in its simplest form.
maths.answer: 3 tenths ran off and 7 tenths were held back.
maths.explain: 60 out of 200 is 60 over 200. Dividing top and bottom by 20 gives 3 over 10. The rest, 10 tenths take away 3 tenths, is 7 tenths.
maths.context: In the Forest Floor Test, you measure how much of the rain runs off each plate.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets us compare plates even if the amount of rain changes between tests.

maths.problem: In the Blanket Test, suppose the dry layer in the bare cup measured 0, 1, 2 and 3 centimetres on days 1 to 4, and the dry layer in the cup with leaves measured 0, 0, 1 and 1 centimetres. If each cup keeps drying at the same pace, on which day does each cup first have a dry layer of 5 centimetres?
maths.answer: The bare cup reaches 5 centimetres on day 6. The leaf cup reaches it on about day 11, which is twice as long.
maths.explain: The bare cup grows 1 centimetre a day, so day 4 is 3 centimetres, day 5 is 4 and day 6 is 5. The leaf cup grows about 1 centimetre every 2 days after day 2, so it reaches 5 centimetres at about day 11. This is a guess from the pattern on a line graph.
maths.context: In the Blanket Test, you measure how deep the dry layer is in cups of soil each day.
maths.why_maths: A pattern of daily measurements lets us predict ahead and compare how fast two things change.

maths.problem: A pond holds 24 fish. Each year the villagers take 8 fish. Then the fish that are left have young, and the number of new fish is half the number that were left. How many fish are there after the new fish arrive, in year 1 and in year 2? What if the villagers take 12 fish each year instead: in which year is the pond empty?
maths.answer: With 8 taken the pond has 24 fish after year 1 and 24 after year 2, so the pond can last for ever. With 12 taken it has 18 after year 1, 9 after year 2, and in year 3 there are not enough fish to take 12, so the pond is empty.
maths.explain: With 8 taken: 24 minus 8 is 16, and half of 16 is 8, so 16 plus 8 makes 24 again. With 12 taken: 24 minus 12 is 12, plus half of 12 (6) is 18. Next, 18 minus 12 is 6, plus 3 is 9. Next, 9 minus 12 cannot be done, so the pond is empty in year 3.
maths.context: In the Shared Pond game, you take beans, which stand for fish, from a pond that grows back by a rule.
maths.why_maths: Following the numbers year by year shows that a small change in how much we take can be the difference between a pond that lasts and one that empties.

maths.problem: A canal gives 120 minutes of water each morning, shared equally among 8 farming families. How many minutes does each family get? If 2 more families join, how many minutes does each get, and how many fewer is that for each of the first 8 families?
maths.answer: Each of the 8 families gets 15 minutes. With 10 families each gets 12 minutes, which is 3 minutes fewer.
maths.explain: 120 divided by 8 is 15. 120 divided by 10 is 12. 15 take away 12 is 3.
maths.context: In the Shared Pond game, the players share one pond. Here, farmers share a canal.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a shared amount shows what happens to each person's share when more people use the same thing, which is why shared things need rules.

maths.problem: A school roof is 8 metres long and 5 metres wide. One millimetre of rain falling on one square metre gives 1 litre of water. How many litres of water fall on the roof in a shower of 20 millimetres?
maths.explain: The roof area is 8 times 5, which is 40 square metres. Each square metre gets 20 litres. 40 times 20 is 800 litres.
maths.context: In the Slow the Rain challenge, you think about how to catch and slow rain.
maths.why_maths: Finding the area of a roof tells us how much rain we could catch and let sink into the ground instead of running down the street.

maths.problem: On a trail, you find 12 signs. Four show food, 3 show shelter, 2 show travel of seeds, 2 show clean-up and 1 shows a change to the place. Which link is the most common? What fraction of the signs show food? Draw a bar chart in your notebook.
maths.answer: Food is the most common, with 4 signs. 4 out of 12 is one third of the signs. The bar chart has bars of height 4, 3, 2, 2 and 1.
maths.explain: The biggest number is 4, which is food. 4 out of 12 simplifies to 1 out of 3. A bar chart puts each link on the bottom and the number of signs up the side.
maths.context: On a Window Trail, you tally the signs of life you find, and the link each one shows.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart makes it easy to see which kind of link you found most, and a fraction tells how large a share of all the signs it is.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1968 an American biologist named Garrett Hardin wrote an essay called The Tragedy of the Commons. He pictured a field that every herder shares. Each herder gains by adding one more cow, he said, so all of them add cows until the grass is gone. Many people took this to mean that shared land and water are always ruined, unless someone owns them or a government rules them. Elinor Ostrom, a political scientist, wondered whether it was true. She and her students gathered real cases: mountain meadows in Switzerland, forests in Japan, irrigation canals in Spain and the Philippines. Many had been shared for hundreds of years and were still healthy. The villagers had made rules about who could take how much, watched each other, and warned and fined cheats. Her 1990 book, Governing the Commons, showed that people can look after a shared thing if they make the rules together. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics.
how_we_found_out.who: Elinor Ostrom, an American political scientist (1933 to 2012), who tested the idea of Garrett Hardin
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people believed that a shared field, forest or pond is always used up, because each person gains by taking a bit more. Ostrom showed that many villages had kept shared things safe for centuries, by making and keeping their own rules.

quiz: Dead leaves on forest soil help the ground soak up rain and let it go slowly.
Leaf litter, roots and soil animals together make gaps that hold water like a sponge.
Sweeping the ground bare makes forest soil healthier and keeps more water.
Bare soil dries out and washes away, while leaf litter keeps soil damp and feeds worms and fungi.
A layer of mulch keeps soil damp for longer than bare soil.
Mulch covers the soil, so less water is lost to the sun and wind.
A forest is one living body, with all its plants and animals sharing one goal.
Each plant and animal lives by her own needs, and they do not share a body or a goal.
No single leaf, root or worm holds the rain; the holding comes from all of them together.
Each does a small job, and only together do they make a floor that soaks up water.
Shared forests and ponds are always ruined unless someone owns them or a government rules them.
Many shared meadows, forests and canals have lasted hundreds of years under rules the villagers made and kept.
Plants send most of the water their roots drink out into the air as vapour.
This is transpiration, and the vapour rises and may fall again as rain.
Sacred groves protect all the nature around them.
Many groves are small and shrinking, and the land around them is often cleared.
Earthworms and termites change the soil and land where they live.
They dig and mix the ground, which changes how water and living things use the place.
Taking as many fish as you can each day is sustainable.
Sustainable means taking no faster than the fish grow back, so enough is left for the future.
odd: Earthworms, termites and elephants change soil or land so much that others find new homes; a dragonfly does not.
Leaf litter, roots and tunnels let rain soak in; bare baked ground sends it running off downhill.
A track, a dropping and a web are signs left behind by living beings; a pebble is not.
The first three are shared by a whole community; a pencil box belongs to one person.
The first three take things no faster than they grow back; felling a whole hillside leaves nothing to grow back.
